narrative:
I am Ananthi Ammal, and I need your help regarding my land. I own a piece of agricultural land in my village in Tamil Nadu. It’s about one acre, and it has been with my family for a long time. I have the patta in my name, and I’ve been paying land tax regularly. This land is my only source of income.

In 1978, the government passed a new rule saying they could take land for building house sites or other facilities for people from certain communities. I didn’t know about this law until one day, I found out that a notice had been published in the local government paper saying my land was being taken. The notice said the Collector had decided to acquire it for one of these welfare schemes. I was never asked beforehand, never given a chance to speak, and no one came to inspect the land or talk to me.

What’s worse is that the moment the notice came out, the law says the land now belongs to the government, completely and without any claim from me—even though I’ve done nothing wrong and have all the documents. They say I’ll get money for it, based on the market value on the date of the notice, but it won’t be paid all at once. If the amount is more than Rs. 2,000, they will pay it in yearly parts, over up to five years. That doesn’t help me, because I need the money now to survive.

If I don’t agree with how much they’re offering, I can raise an issue, but only about a small part of the payment. And even that goes to a court, which will follow their own process. I feel this is not fair. They could have used the old way of taking land, which at least lets people object and have their say. This new method feels one-sided and harsh.

I didn’t do anything to lose my land. I’ve always paid my dues and lived peacefully. I want either my land back, or to be paid fairly and fully at once, after a proper process where I can speak. I need your help to make this right.

My name is Sulochana Amma. I am the daughter of Kutty Ammna, who passed away in 1971. On May 19, 1961, my mother made a settlement deed giving her husband, Krishnan Nair (K), the right to live on and use her property during his lifetime. After he passed away, the property was to come to me. That document is in my possession and clearly says I am the rightful owner once his life interest ends.

After my mother died, K had no right to sell the property — he could only use it while he was alive. But in 1972, he sold it to two men named Narayanan Nair and Chennan through a registered sale deed. I found out about this and took action right away. I went to the local court and filed a case to stop him from selling or damaging the land. In 1975, the court ruled that K had no right to sell and ordered him not to interfere with the property.

Later, in 1975, a third person bought the property from Narayanan Nair and Chennan. He was not part of my first case, but he started trying to take control and make changes to the land. So I filed another case against both K and this new person, and in 1981, the court again said they had no right to interfere and stopped them from doing anything to the property. At that time, they did not decide whether this new buyer had any claim, but they made it clear that K had no right to transfer ownership.

In 1982, I filed another case asking for a clear declaration that I am the rightful owner and that this third person has no claim over the land. That case was decided in my favour. The decision was later confirmed by a higher court.

Now, this third person is still claiming he owns the property because he bought it from the people K sold to. But that sale was based on a right K never had. I have the original settlement deed from 1961, copies of all the notices I filed, and the orders from the cases I won. I want to stop him for good. I need to prove that I am the true owner and that he cannot claim anything through a sale that was invalid from the start.

I am the managing director of Neyvely Lignite Corporation Ltd., a company set up by the government to mine lignite coal in South Arcot District, Tamil Nadu. In 1975, the government announced it would take over about 5,200 acres of land in that area so we could carry out excavation work. The land was being taken for our use, to support the coal mining project we were running.

Over the next few years, a local revenue officer started deciding how much money should be paid to the people who owned the land. Between 1977 and 1980, he gave out compensation amounts, but many of the landowners were not happy with what they were offered. More than 2,000 of them went to the civil court asking for higher payments. In some cases, the court has already decided on new amounts and issued final orders.

Since our company will have to pay for whatever compensation is finally decided, we thought it only fair that we should be able to take part in the ongoing cases. We wanted to give evidence, especially to make sure the amounts being awarded are reasonable and not too high, and also to confirm that the land being taken is clear of disputes and encumbrances. So we asked to be included as a party in those pending cases.

But our request was turned down. We were told we don’t have the right to be part of these proceedings. Later, when the state government challenged some of the higher compensation decisions, we again asked to be included — but that was also refused. We even approached the higher court directly, saying the awards were not correct, but they said we don’t have the authority to raise such issues.

We’re not trying to take the land or stop anyone from getting their due. But since we’re the ones who will have to pay the final price, we believe we should have a chance to speak up and make sure things are done fairly. We just want to be heard before large sums are fixed that we’ll have to bear.

I own a piece of agricultural land in one of the villages in Delhi. It’s about half a bigha, maybe a little more. My family has been farming it for years, and it’s been in my name for as long as I can remember. I have the revenue records that show I’m the owner, and I’ve always paid the land taxes on time.

In late 1980, I saw a government notice saying they were planning to take a large amount of land from our area — including our village — for city development. The notice said that some lands would be left out, like government land or plots that already had building plans approved by the Municipal Corporation before November 1980. Our land was none of those — it was just farmland, so it wasn’t exempt.

After that, nothing happened for years. No one came to survey, no one talked to us, and no official action was taken. I assumed maybe they weren’t going to take our land after all.

But then, in 1985 — more than four years later — they suddenly issued another notice saying the acquisition was now final. That’s when I got worried. I found out from others that there was supposed to be a time limit for this kind of thing — that once the first notice came out, the next step had to happen within three years. But here it was, 1985, and they were only now completing the process. The last of these final notices didn’t even come until early 1986.

I later heard that some other landowners had gone to court soon after the first notice and got orders to stop the process. But I didn’t know I needed to do that at the time. I didn’t file anything back then. I only tried to raise my concern later, but by then, the authorities said it was too late.

I didn’t do anything wrong. I’ve always been the rightful owner, in possession, and paying my dues. The government waited too long to act. I want them to recognize that this delay makes the takeover invalid, and I want my land back. I just want a fair chance to keep what’s rightfully mine.

I bought a house at 64, Lloyds Road, Royaspettah, Madras-14, on 23 October 1967. I bought it because I needed a place to live. At that time, the house was occupied by R. M. Seshadri, who had been renting it from the previous owner. After I bought the property, he started paying rent to me, so from then on, he was my tenant.

I told him in writing on 27 January 1968 that I needed the house for myself and asked him to leave by 29 February 1968. I gave two notices—one said 28 February and the other said 29 February—just to be safe, in case there was any issue with the date. In those letters, I explained that I had no other house in Madras and that I had been asked to vacate my own rented home at No. 2, Lakshmipuram, 1st Street, Madras-14, and had to move out by 27 January 1969. So I really needed this house to stay in.

But he didn’t leave. So I decided to take action. I went to the local court handling rent matters and told them I needed him to vacate because I had no other home and was being forced out of my own rented place. He responded by saying he wasn’t the tenant—that a partnership firm called M/s. R. M. Seshadri was the real tenant. He also said I didn’t actually need the house, that I wasn’t being honest about why I wanted it, and that I had no right to ask him to leave. He claimed the firm had spent a lot of money on repairs because the old owner had promised they could stay forever.

I went and gave my side in person. I told them I bought the house for my own use, that I had nowhere else to live, and that I was being evicted from my rented place. I showed many documents—about 45 of them—including a copy of the order that said I had to vacate my old house by January 1969. He didn’t question me or challenge any of the documents I showed.

Then, on 31 March 1969, he agreed in writing to give up his defence, to leave the house by 5 June 1969, and not to ask for more time. I agreed to give him that date to move out. On the same day, I paid him Rs. 20,000 towards the repairs he said he had done. He also wrote me a letter confirming he would leave by 5 June and that he had received the money.

But now he’s still not leaving. He’s ignoring the agreement we both signed. I want him to finally vacate and hand over the house to me. I need the place for myself and have waited long enough.

I am the Delhi Development Authority, and I need your help to reclaim a piece of land that was sold without any legal right. The plot is number 3 in the Industrial Area Scheme on Najafgarh Road, New Delhi. It’s 2044.4 square yards and is Nazul land, which means it belongs to the government and we manage it.

In 1957, we made an agreement with a company called M/s Mehta Constructions. The agreement said they could lease the plot, but only after they met certain conditions and signed a final lease deed. That final lease deed was never signed. There was a clause in the agreement that clearly said until the lease deed was executed and registered, they wouldn’t have any right, title, or interest in the land. Since that never happened, they never legally held the plot.

But in 1972, they went ahead and signed an agreement to sell the plot to another company, M/s Pure Drinks Private Limited, for Rs. 3,06,700. Then, in 1985, a sale deed was registered in favour of Pure Drinks. I later found out that someone connected to Mehta Constructions told a court official to go to the sub-registrar and register the sale, but the official didn’t know that Mehta Constructions had no legal right over the land in the first place.

Later, Pure Drinks went into liquidation, and in 2000, the plot was put up for auction. Another company, S.G.G. Towers Pvt. Ltd., bought it. They applied to confirm the sale later that year, and we objected at that time, saying the original company never had any right to the land, so nothing could be sold.

I know that for Nazul land like this, any transfer requires our prior approval, which was never given. The rules also say unearned income must be paid when such transfers happen, but even that wasn’t settled properly.

I want to stop this company from claiming ownership and get the land back under our control. The entire sale chain is based on a title that never existed, and I want that corrected.

I sold a piece of land in village Khirki, Malviya Nagar, New Delhi—Plot No. 148—in September 2002 to a man named Mohd. Yusuf for ₹2.10 lakh, and we got the sale deed registered. After that, he went to court in April 2003, saying I was trying to throw him out. I responded and went to the court on 29 April 2003. I told them clearly that I had sold the property and handed it over, but he still owed me ₹25,000. I also said I had not threatened him or tried to remove him, and I wouldn’t do so. His lawyer accepted what I said, and the court closed the case on 12 May 2003, noting that I had promised not to interfere with his possession.

Later, in August 2003, my son filed a case asking for a share in Plot No. 148 and another plot, 147A, saying he had rights over them. Then, Mohd. Yusuf went back to court and claimed that in August 2003, he found the locks broken at the property and blamed me and my family. I replied that the sale was not fair—it was done under fraud—and I wanted to cancel it. In February 2004, the court said I had said different things at different times and passed the matter to a higher court, saying I might have broken my promise.

I filed a new case in February 2005 to cancel the sale deed. But later, I was told that a higher court had decided I had broken my word and sentenced me to four months in jail. I never got a proper chance to explain my side. I didn’t get any notice before this decision. I only wanted to challenge a sale I now believe was not valid. I didn’t do anything wrong, and I shouldn’t be punished like this. I want this punishment taken back.

I am Sayyed Ali, and my family has been living on and managing a large piece of land in Devada Mokhasa village, Visakhapatnam, for as long as anyone can remember. The land is about 358 acres, and it’s been passed down through my ancestors. It’s recorded under Title Deed No. 42, and we’ve always known it was given to our forefathers by the old government—before independence—for the purpose of supporting the Dargah of Syed Ali Ishaq Madina Vali. But it wasn’t given to the Dargah directly. It was given to specific people, including my ancestors, on the condition that they perform services there and spend part of the income on the Dargah’s upkeep, Moharram festivals, repairs, and charity to poor Muslims and travelling fakirs.

Every year, my family has set aside money for these purposes, and we’ve kept records showing how the money was spent. We were told long ago that if we stopped doing the work or failed to spend the money properly, the government could take the land back. That’s how it was always understood—this was a grant tied to service, not outright ownership by a religious body.

In the 1960s, the local revenue officer looked into the status of the land and confirmed it was inam land—land granted for service—and that it was not held by any institution. That finding was later upheld by a higher revenue authority. But later, the Andhra Pradesh Wakf Board claimed this land as their own, saying it was wakf property. They put out a public notice in 1961 saying so, even though no document from the time of the original grant calls it a wakf.

Now they’re saying that because it’s wakf, my family has no right to manage it or give leases to others. But we’ve been doing this for generations. We have old records, including government revenue entries, that show the land was granted to individuals like my ancestors, not dedicated permanently to the Dargah. I want to protect our family’s right to continue managing this land as long as we fulfill the duties connected to it. I don’t believe the Wakf Board should be able to take it away just because they say it belongs to them.

I need your help because I’ve been thrown off land that’s been in my family for years, and I don’t know how to get it back. The property is in Jamshedpur, and it all started with my father, Gopal Singh. In February 1971, a company called Engineers Syndicate (India) Private Limited borrowed Rs. 14,571 from him. As security, they gave him the sale documents for a piece of land and handed over physical possession of it the next day, treating that as interest on the loan.  

When they didn’t repay, they agreed to sell the land to my father for Rs. 25,000. He paid the remaining Rs. 10,429 after adjusting the loan amount, and they signed a written agreement to sell. But they never completed the sale. So in 1974, my father went to the local civil court in Jamshedpur and filed a case to claim ownership. The court ruled in his favour in May 1977. Then, in October 1982, the sale was officially completed through the court, and my father was put in possession by a court officer.  

After he passed away, my brother and I took over. We’ve been in continuous possession ever since, treating it as our own. But in April 2008, we were suddenly thrown out. A man named Abdul Rafai showed up with a court officer and took control of the land on 27 April 2008. We had no warning.  

Later, we found out that years earlier, another company had won a money judgment against Engineers Syndicate in Calcutta. That judgment was transferred to someone named Abdul Rab in 2005. He then pushed for the land to be attached and sold to recover the debt. But that shouldn’t have included this property—my father had already won it in court, and back in 1982, when the Calcutta court had tried to attach it, he had objected and they removed it from the list. That fact was never disclosed.  

Abdul Rab got the land attached again, it was auctioned, and Abdul Rafai—who we believe is connected to him—bought it. We filed a request with the local court asking to be given back possession and to stop them from treating the land as theirs. But the court said it couldn’t look into the matter. I have the 1982 sale document, the 1977 court order in my father’s favour, and proof we’ve been living on and managing the land for decades. I just want to get our property back and stop this fraud.

I own a small shop, Shop No. 408, in Pandit Lila Ram Market, Masjid Moth, New Delhi. I bought it many years ago and have always managed it myself. In the late 1970s, I gave the shop on rent to Mr. Vasdev. He was supposed to pay me every month, but from January 1980, he stopped paying anything. I waited for a long time, hoping he would clear the dues, but nothing came.

So on May 18, 1981, I sent him a written notice demanding all the unpaid rent. He didn’t pay, and he didn’t even respond. After two months passed with no payment, I went to the office that handles rent matters and filed a case asking to get my shop back because he hadn’t paid.

In January 1984, the officer there gave an order saying Vasdev had to pay all the arrears—Rs. 50 per month from January 1980—within one month. He also had to keep paying the monthly rent on time after that, by the 15th of each month. He paid me only Rs. 500, and said he would clear the rest soon, but he never did. He missed the deadline and didn’t pay the next months’ rent either.

Since he didn’t follow the order, I went back and asked that he no longer be allowed to defend himself in the case, because he had broken the terms. The officer first agreed and said he must vacate the shop. But later, he changed his decision, saying there might have been some understanding between us and that the delay wasn’t serious. I never agreed to any delay or compromise. He still hasn’t paid me the full amount.

Now he’s still sitting in my shop, not paying properly, and I’m getting nothing. I’ve lost years of rent and can’t use the shop myself or give it to someone else. I just want him to leave so I can take back what’s mine. I need your help to make that happen.

I am a trustee of the Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust. The trust was created in 1927 by Lala Kharaiti Ram of Lahore through his will. He wanted to promote Sanskrit education and improve Ayurvedic medicine, and one of the ways to do that was by running a hospital. We had a hospital in Lahore, but after Partition in 1947, we had to leave Pakistan and come to India as refugees. We lost everything.

In 1951, the government gave us nine acres of land in Lajpat Nagar, Delhi, so we could rebuild the hospital here. At that time, Lajpat Nagar was not a developed or expensive area. The land was given to help us restart our hospital work in India after being displaced. We built Moolchand Hospital on this land and have been running it since then.

When we were given the land, there was no condition that we must provide free treatment to a fixed number of poor patients. The letter giving us the land did not say that. Later, a 99-year lease was signed with the President of India, starting from April 17, 1951. That lease also did not have any such condition.

Now, in 2012, the Delhi government has sent a circular saying that because we got land from the government, we must give free treatment to 10% of our indoor patients and 25% of our outdoor patients who are poor. This order came years after we started the hospital and after the lease was signed. We were never told about this rule when we got the land. We were never part of any discussion or decision that led to this.

We do help poor patients. Since 1958, our specialist doctors have been spending one hour every day treating poor OPD patients for free. But we cannot accept a new condition being added to our lease suddenly, especially one that was never agreed upon. The government should not be able to change the terms like this after so many years.

I want to stop them from forcing us to follow this rule. We want to keep running the hospital the way we always have — serving the public without making a profit, but without being bound by new conditions we never signed up for.

I am the owner of one acre of wetland in Ayanambakkam, Ambattur, part of survey numbers 287 and 288. The total land is 1.80 acres, and I’ve owned this piece for many years. On 5 October 1989, I signed an agreement with Mr. S. Sambandan to sell him this one acre for Rs. 6.5 lakh. On that day, he gave me Rs. 50,000 in cash as advance payment, which I accepted. The agreement clearly said we had to complete the sale within six months — by April 1990.

After that, I kept trying to move things forward. I called him and asked him to pay the remaining Rs. 6 lakh and come to complete the sale, but he didn’t respond. I even sent him a registered letter on 17 March 1990, asking him to execute a power of attorney so we could proceed, but he never replied. Then, on 26 March 1990, I got a legal notice from his lawyer, but I refused to accept it — the post office returned it. Later, I saw notices he published in *Dhina Thanthi* and *Indian Express* in May 1990, warning people not to buy this land from me. That’s when I realised he was trying to stop me from selling to anyone else, even though he wasn’t doing his part.

He never paid the balance amount. He never showed me any proof that he had the money or that he was ready to pay. He didn’t deposit the remaining amount anywhere. And he only came to court on 26 March 1993 — more than three years after our agreement.

I was always ready and willing to sell the land as agreed. I tried to contact him, I followed up, but he ignored me. Now he’s asking the court to force me to sell, even though he didn’t fulfill his responsibilities. I want to stop this case and protect my right to sell the land freely. I also want to be compensated for the years I’ve lost because he blocked my property without completing the deal.

Back in 1987, the Bihar government issued a public notice saying they were taking over our agricultural land in Mouza Sansarpur and Hardas Chak. The notice came on 18th November, and just a few days later, on 24th November, they said the acquisition was urgent and that they were taking immediate possession. They claimed the land was needed to build homes for senior state officers. At the same time, they announced that the usual process where landowners get to raise objections would not apply to us. I never got any chance to speak or object.

They moved in quickly and took control of the land. Over the years, they paid me about 80% of what they said the land was worth. I have receipts showing these payments, but the full amount was never settled. The remaining 20%, along with proper interest for such a long delay, has not been paid. I still have my original land records proving I was the owner.

What hurts more is that a large part of the land they took has been lying unused for decades. It’s not being used for housing at all. Some portions are now being used as helipads for state officials, which was never mentioned when they took the land. If they don’t need it for the purpose they said, then why are they still holding on to it?

Later, I heard that there was some kind of direction from a higher authority that they had to complete the compensation process and pass a formal decision on the value. But nothing happened. They took our land, paid us only part of what we’re owed, and then just stopped doing anything.

I want them to finally complete the compensation process, pay me the full amount with fair interest, and if they don’t need the land anymore, give it back. We’ve waited over thirty years. I just want justice.

I own a building called Atma Ram Mansion on Connaught Circus in New Delhi, which I bought through a registered sale deed in 1980. One portion of this building has been rented out to a tenant – Oriental Insurance Company – for a long time. Their monthly rent was Rs.1,438, and they were also paying service tax of Rs.148, making the total payment Rs.1,586 per month. This rent has not increased in years, and the tenancy has been governed under the Delhi Rent Control Act, which protects tenants as long as the rent doesn’t go above Rs.3,500 per month.

In 2009, the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) changed how property tax is calculated. Instead of being based on rent, it started using the unit area system. Because of this, the annual property tax on the premises occupied by the tenant shot up to over Rs.9.6 lakh per year – that’s about Rs.80,000 per month. Under the NDMC Act, this tax is supposed to be recoverable from the tenant as arrears of rent. I sent multiple notices to the tenant in July 2009 and December 2009 asking them to pay their share of the tax, but they didn’t respond or make any payment.

Since I’m the owner, NDMC held me responsible. To avoid penalties, I had to pay over Rs.2.9 crore in property tax myself by 2010. I sent another notice in April 2010 asking the tenant to reimburse me, but it was returned undelivered. Then, in June 2010, I formally terminated their tenancy, stating that since the rent plus recoverable tax now exceeds Rs.3,500 per month, they no longer have protection under the Rent Control Act.

The tenant replied in July 2010, saying they don’t owe the tax and that they’re still protected under the Rent Act. They refuse to vacate. I want to take back possession of the property and also claim compensation for the time they’ve stayed without paying their dues. My understanding is that the law allows me to treat this tax as part of the rent, and once that’s added, the threshold is crossed. I need your help to move forward with a case for possession and recovery.

I’m Shiv Raj, and my family has been farming land in Chhatarpur village for generations. We’ve always been recognised as the rightful holders of this land in the government revenue records. The total area is about 50,000 bighas, and it’s been our livelihood for as long as I can remember.  

In 1980, the government put up a public notice saying they were taking over our land for the development of Delhi. I didn’t agree with it, so I raised my objection formally, along with other farmers from the village. We were told we’d get a chance to present our side, and a government officer held a hearing where we spoke against the takeover. But before he could submit his report, he was transferred out.  

Then, a new officer took over—someone who had not heard us or seen our evidence. He went ahead and approved the acquisition without calling us again or giving us another hearing. We were never given a chance to speak before the final decision was made.  

Later, we were served a notice saying the land was officially being taken, and an amount was set for compensation. But we never accepted that process because it wasn’t fair. We had already started raising our concerns with the authorities, saying the decision was made by someone who didn’t hear us, which made it wrong in principle.  

For years, nothing was settled. The government never took physical possession of the land, and we continued to live and work on it. We’ve been here all along, undisturbed. In 2013, I heard that a new land acquisition rule came in, and under it, old cases like ours—where no possession was taken and no compensation was paid—can no longer be pursued.  

I want to make sure that our rights are protected. The land belongs to us, and we never gave up our claim. I want to stop the government from trying to take it now, after so many years, especially through a process that ignored our right to be heard. I want to be able to continue living and farming on this land without any threat hanging over us.

My name is Ratan Lal Sharma, and I need your help with a business matter that went wrong. In December 1962, I started a business called New Bengal Engineering Works with my partner, Purshottam Harit. We set up a factory, bought some land, and acquired machinery and tools. We both invested money and ran the business together as partners.

But within six months, we began having serious disagreements. We couldn’t agree on how to manage things, and the partnership broke down. To avoid a long fight, we both agreed in writing on August 22, 1963, to let two people—Sri R.N. Sharma and Sri C.M. Sharma—decide our disputes. We gave them full authority to settle everything between us.

They looked into our issues and gave their decision on September 20, 1963. Their award clearly divided the business, including the factory and the land, and assigned me a specific share of the property and assets. I have a copy of that award, and I know the arbitrators sent it to the authorities as required.

Now, Purshottam is refusing to follow what was decided. He won’t let me take possession of my share of the land or the business property. He’s saying the decision can’t be enforced because it wasn’t registered, since it involves property. But we both agreed to this process, and the decision was made fairly.

I have the written agreement we signed for arbitration and the award document. I just want to get what was rightfully given to me. I don’t want to work with him again—I want to take my share and move on. I need your help to make sure he can’t just ignore this.

I’m Sesh Nath Singh, and I’m a director of a company called Debi Fabtech Private Ltd. We used to export textiles and garments. In February 2012, we approached the Baidyabati Sheoraphuli Co-operative Bank for a loan of one crore rupees. They agreed and gave us the money through a cash credit account—Account No. 482. On 17th February 2012, we signed a document giving them security over our machinery and other movable assets.

By May 2012, we couldn’t keep up with the repayments, and the account stopped being active. The bank marked it as a bad loan on 31st March 2013. Then, in January 2014, they sent us a notice saying we had to pay Rs. 1,07,88,536 within 60 days, or they would take action. We replied in March 2014, explaining why we thought their notice wasn’t valid. But in July 2014, they wrote back saying they were rejecting our reply and demanding payment again.

In December 2014, they sent another notice saying they would take over our factory and equipment if we didn’t pay. Then, later that month, they announced they had already taken possession of our secured assets. Around that time, we raised a concern with a higher authority about whether this bank even has the power to do what they did, because they are a co-operative bank, not a regular commercial bank. We were told they shouldn’t be allowed to act like this.

In May 2017, a local government officer issued an order allowing the bank to keep possession. But a few months later, the higher authority stepped in and told the bank to stop taking any further action while they looked into the matter. That process is still going on.

Then, in July 2018—more than five years after the loan was declared bad—the bank started a new process to take control of our company, saying they want to recover their money through insolvency. I don’t see how this is fair. They waited years, took their own actions, and now want to restart everything. I want to stop this new process because it’s too late for them to come forward, and they’ve already been trying to deal with the matter another way all this time.

I own a piece of land in Delhi that originally belonged to someone named Shri Chand. Back in 1961, the government put out a notice saying they wanted to acquire this land for the planned development of the city. Another notice came in 1969 saying the land was needed for public use. But over the years, no one ever came to take physical control of the land, and there was never any official order saying the acquisition was cancelled.

In June 1980, I bought the land from Shri Chand through his authorized agent, Mr. Nand Kishore. I paid for it, got a proper sale deed, and registered it with the sub-registrar. Before the sale, I made sure to get official permission from the government authority that handles land transfers in Delhi. They gave me a No Objection Certificate, and the sale deed even has a note saying that permission was obtained. After that, my name was entered in the revenue records as the owner.

Later, in 1992, three companies — Sapphire Sales, Zircon Trading, and Eternal Agencies — bought nearby plots from the legal heirs of another original owner, Shri Khyali Ram. They also have registered sale deeds and have been in possession of their land.

But in 1997, the government passed an award saying the land had been acquired. Then in January 2000, they claimed they had taken possession, which we don’t accept — no one removed us or took over the site.

Now they’re saying my purchase isn’t valid because the land was under acquisition when I bought it. But I acted in good faith. I followed all the rules, got the required approvals, registered the sale, and updated the records. I want the government to recognize my ownership, or if they insist on keeping the land, to give me alternative land or fair compensation. I shouldn’t lose everything just because I bought land legally, with all the right permissions, years ago.

My name is Ashiyal Beevi. I want to talk to you about a piece of land in Tirunelveli that belonged to my grandmother, Fathima Beevi. She got it from her father a long time ago through a gift, and we have the document to prove it. It’s about half an acre, and it’s been in our family for years.

In 1982, my grandmother signed another gift deed in favour of Khaja Mohideen, who was married to one of her daughter-in-laws — the first woman I’m dealing with now. But that wasn’t a fair deal. He lived with my grandmother and took advantage of her. She was old and alone, and he pressured her into signing. She never meant to give him the land, and nothing changed after that — she still treated it as hers.

Khaja Mohideen died in 1988, before my grandmother. After he passed, nothing happened with that 1982 gift. Then, in 1990, my grandmother sold the entire property to me through a registered sale deed on 14 November. I paid her the full amount, and it was properly recorded. She was healthy and clear in her mind when we did it.

After she passed away, I expected to take over the property. But the first woman and her children — the other people involved — refused to leave. They say the 1982 gift gives them rights, even though their husband and father died before my grandmother, and she clearly sold it to me later.

I went to a local court in 1992 to ask for recognition of my ownership and to get possession. The person hearing the matter said the 1982 gift wasn’t valid and that my 1990 sale was real, but still only said I could have one-sixth of the land. That doesn’t make sense — if the earlier gift doesn’t count and I bought the whole thing, why don’t I get it all?

I asked again for that decision to be looked at, but they said no in 2006. I believe there’s a clear mistake — they accepted my sale was valid but didn’t give me full rights. I want to be recognized as the full owner of the property and to finally get possession from them. That’s what I’m hoping to achieve.

Back in January 2007, my company, Chemplast Cuddalore Vinyls Limited, entered into an agreement with a woman named Senthamizh Selvi to buy one acre of land in Thiyagavalli village, Cuddalore. The total price was Rs. 1.5 lakh, which we paid in full. She handed over possession of the land to us at that time. On 26th March 2007, she gave us a registered Power of Attorney, naming us as her agents to complete all formalities for the sale, including getting the sale deed registered. Then, on 7th September 2007, we got the sale agreement itself registered at the sub-registrar’s office in Cuddalore.

But things started going wrong. In November 2007, she sent a letter saying she was canceling the Power of Attorney. We replied right away, telling her that the agreement was still valid and we expected her to follow through. Then, in February 2008, she sent another letter and included a demand draft for Rs. 1.5 lakh. The letter said the money was being returned because she had borrowed it from us to buy a vehicle. But that wasn’t true — this was clearly the sale amount. We sent the draft back and told her again that we wanted the sale completed. On 9th February 2008, we formally notified her to execute the sale deed and not transfer the land to anyone else. She never replied.

We went to the sub-registrar several times to register the sale deed, but they refused. We were told that since the land was in Thiyagavalli, no private sale could be registered because of an old government order that reserved the area for a power project. We later found out that another company had been given special permission to develop a power plant there and could buy land, but we couldn’t.

By mid-February 2008, we noticed that Senthamizh Selvi and that other company were trying to take control of the land. They were coming onto the property and acting like they had rights over it. To protect ourselves, we filed a case on 16th February 2008 in the district court in Cuddalore, asking the court to stop them from interfering with our possession.

Now that the government order blocking sales has been removed, I want to move forward and get the sale deed executed. I want the court to make her complete the sale as per our agreement. That’s what I need your help with.

I own two shops in Delhi that have been in my family for a long time. My father, Haji Badrul Islam, originally owned them and gave them on oral lease to the current tenant back in 1970. After my father passed away, I inherited the property. I also got a legal award dated 11th March 1980 that confirmed my ownership. My father passed away after that, and then my brother Sajid-Ul-Islam, who was also a legal heir, managed the property until he died on 21st November 1986. Since then, I’ve been the rightful owner by inheritance and under the award.

The tenant has been running his business from these shops for over 50 years now. In 2014, I applied to get the shops back because I need them for my own use. I don’t have any other suitable place to run my business, and I’ve been clear about that. The tenant responded saying he should be allowed to defend, claiming three things: first, that I don’t have proper title; second, that the government took over the property because some relatives live in Pakistan; and third, that I have other properties that I could use instead.

I’ve denied having any other suitable business premises. The officer who handles rent matters looked at all this and agreed with me — he said the tenant can’t challenge my ownership, especially since he’s been paying rent all these years, and that the claim about alternative properties is vague. He also said the government takeover doesn’t apply here.

But the tenant went to a higher authority and got permission to defend the case, saying there are “triable issues” about whether I really need the shops and whether I have other properties. I don’t understand how that’s fair. I’ve already explained my position clearly. The tenant has also started some new proceedings under a newer government law, but those were initiated without proper authority — an earlier inquiry into that matter was already closed in 2015. I even have a report from 4th November 2015 supporting that. There’s also a pending case where it’s already been said that no action should be taken against me, and the tenant tried to join that case but was rejected.

I just want to get back my shops. I’ve waited long enough. I need them for my livelihood, and I have no other suitable place. I want things to move forward so I can finally take possession.

My name is Surendra Pal. My father, Bhim Sain Arora, passed away in January 1964. He had a house and other properties in Calcutta, and he also ran a business. He was married to my mother first, and they had five of us—four daughters and me, the only son. My mother passed away in 1959. After that, my father lived alone for a while.  

Two of my sisters were already married and living with their husbands. Shanta, another sister, was 22 and still unmarried at the time of my father’s death. The youngest, Rita, was only 13 and studying at a school in Simla. I was not staying with my father then—we weren’t on good terms, and I had been living separately.  

In late 1960, my father placed an ad in a newspaper looking for a wife. A woman named Saraswati, who was a doctor, responded. She came to Calcutta in January 1961 with her family. Within a week, they got married on February 7, 1961. I later found out the marriage notice was backdated because they didn’t wait the required time.  

The very next day, February 8, my father went to the house of Saraswati’s brother-in-law, a man named Colonel Vigh. There, he signed a will that left everything to Saraswati. The will was witnessed by Colonel Vigh and another man, Nelson Das, who I was told worked at a company. I don’t know how they were chosen.  

After my father died, I wrote to Saraswati. I had never heard of this will. I asked to see it. I also said that if there was no will, we should divide the property among all of us—his children and his mother. But she didn’t respond to that. Instead, she started legal steps to claim everything.  

We believe this will was not made freely. My father had known Saraswati for only a few days when he signed it. He didn’t talk to any lawyer. He didn’t discuss it with any of us. His own mother, Wazir Devi, says she knew nothing about it. After the death, she was made to leave the house and had to come stay with me.  

I want this will to be set aside. It’s not right that someone who came into his life so suddenly gets everything, while his own children and mother get nothing. I want our fair share of what belongs to us.

I own a multi-storey building in Calcutta that I constructed after 1956. The building is fully rented out, and I have agreements with all the tenants based on the rent we mutually agreed at the time of letting. No authority has stepped in to fix or control the rent under any tenancy law — it’s just the rent we settled on between us.

In October 1966, I got a notice from the local municipal body saying they had assessed the annual value of my property at Rs. 63,365 for property tax purposes. I didn’t agree with that figure, so I filed an objection. The assessing officer later reduced it to Rs. 49,368, but I still felt it was too high because it seemed to be based on the rent I’m actually getting from tenants.

I believe the correct way to value the property for tax should be based on what’s called “fair rent” under the tenancy law that applies to buildings like mine. Since my building was built after 1956, the law says fair rent should be worked out using the actual cost of construction, the market value of the land at the time, and a portion of the annual taxes. That calculation — not the actual rent I collect — should be the basis for setting the annual value.

To prove how much it cost to build the property, I wanted to bring in a qualified valuer to give a proper estimate. At first, the officer handling my appeal refused to let me present that evidence, saying it wasn’t needed. Later, after a similar matter was looked at in another city and a decision came out supporting the idea that fair rent should be the basis, the officer changed their mind and allowed me to bring in the valuer.

But then the municipal body objected again and got that decision overturned, arguing that since no authority has fixed a rent for my building, the tax should be based on what I’m actually receiving from tenants.

I have all the records — construction bills, rental agreements, receipts, and all the notices I’ve received over the years. I just want the tax to be calculated fairly, based on the method the law provides for buildings like mine. That means using the fair rent formula, not the actual rent.

My name is Leela Rajagopal, and I’m one of the daughters of Janaki Amma, who passed away in 1991. She had five sons and two daughters—me and my sister Kamala. I died before her, in 1975, so my side is being represented by my son and family.

Our mother owned a house at No. 8, Malony Road, T. Nagar, Chennai. In December 1981, she made a Will leaving that house to my daughter Geetha and my sister Kamala. At that time, she mentioned having four sons. But just a few weeks later, on 11 January 1982, she made another Will, replacing the first one. In this new Will, she said she had five sons and left the house only to Kamala and Geetha, leaving out all her sons.

We don’t accept that second Will. Right before the first Will, on 10 December 1981, our mother wrote a letter to one of her sons, Thangamani, saying she wanted to divide the house equally among all her children. That shows she wasn’t planning to exclude anyone.

Kamala had come from Tirupathi to stay with our mother just before the second Will was made. She was heavily involved in getting it signed and registered. One of the witnesses was her colleague, and the other witness hasn’t come forward at all. The original Will has never been shown—Kamala says it’s lost, but we find that hard to believe. There’s also confusion about where it was signed. In one place, it says it was done at home, but later it’s said to have been done at the registrar’s office.

Our mother didn’t know English well. The Will was in English, and no one has proved that it was read out to her in a language she understood, or that she knew what she was signing.

We always had a good relationship with our mother. One of my brothers took care of her in her old age. There was no falling out, no reason for her to cut out her sons and one daughter’s family.

I want the Will dated 11 January 1982 to be set aside. The house should be shared equally among all her legal heirs, as it would be if there were no Will. That’s only fair.

I am Pratap Karan, and I want to set things right regarding a piece of land in Nadergul Village, Saroornagar Mandal, Rangareddy District. The land is Survey No. 613, and it originally belonged to my great-uncle, Raja Shivraj Dharmavanth Bahadur. He was the pattadar and full owner of this land. After he passed away in 1917 without any children, a royal order from the Nizam gave his estate to the sons of his two brothers, including my father, Raja Dhiraj Karan. That’s how I became one of the rightful heirs.

The land was surveyed in 1917 (1326 Fasli) and again in 1943 (1352 Fasli). In both records, my great-uncle’s name was shown as the owner in Khata No. 1 and later Khata No. 3. The survey number changed from 579 to 613, but it’s the same land, same boundaries. I have certified copies of the Setwar and Vasul Baqui records from 1943, and they clearly show him as the khatadar. The village map and touch plan also mark the land as “Kancha” belonging to Late Raja.

But something went wrong later. In the 1954–55 Khasra Pahani, there’s a note saying the lands of Late Raja are being shown separately. After that, the revenue records started showing a duplicate Survey No. 119 with over 355 acres marked as “Sarkari Poramboke”, even though the original S.No. 119 was just 1 acre 20 guntas and belonged to someone else, Gaddam Mallaiah. I don’t know how or why this happened, but it looks like the records were tampered with to erase our ownership.

My family and I have always considered this land ours. We tried to get the revenue records corrected under the Andhra Pradesh Record of Right Act, but the authorities refused, saying we need a court declaration first. The government now claims the land became state property after jagirs were abolished in 1949 and that we accepted compensation. But I never received any such payment, and I don’t accept that our private land was taken over. I want the records corrected to show us—the legal heirs—as the rightful owners, and I want to stop anyone from interfering with our rights over this land.

My father, B.P. Sandy, had several children, but when he got older, he decided to give two houses to me and my sister Veronica. The houses are at 22 and 23, Peria Palli Street, Raja Annamalai Puram, Chennai. On 27 August 1981, he made two registered settlement deeds—one giving No. 23 to my sister and No. 22 to me. That was fine at the time. But later, my father realized he had made a mistake. He actually wanted me to have No. 23 and my sister to have No. 22. We all agreed to swap the properties. So on 1 June 1982, my sister and I signed an agreement to exchange them. Two of her colleagues, Sheila Doss and Mrs. Mary Doss, saw us sign it.  

But after that, my sister changed her mind and refused to go through with the exchange. She wouldn’t sign any papers to transfer No. 23 to me. I tried to sort it out, but she wouldn’t cooperate. Then, in October 1983, my father and I signed another document—this one confirmed that No. 23 should be mine, correcting the earlier arrangement. Susan Muthu and A. Bernard witnessed that.  

Later, my sister said the 1982 agreement wasn’t real. She claimed she signed blank stamp papers and was pressured into it. But that’s not true. We were just fixing what my father wanted all along. I even paid off a loan that was taken for her marriage and upkeep, and we had agreed this was part of the understanding.  

I have the original settlement deeds, the 1982 agreement, and the 1983 document my father and I signed. I’ve already sold No. 23 to someone else, based on what we agreed and what my father intended. I just want to make sure that sale is valid and that I’m recognized as the rightful owner of that property. I need help proving that what we did was fair and in line with my father’s real wishes.

My father-in-law, E. Srinivasa Pillai, passed away on 19th January 1978. He had a house at Premises No. 10, Azeez Nagar II Street, Kodambakkam, Chennai, where he lived with our family. Fifteen days before he died, on 4th January 1978, he made a will leaving that house to my husband, S. Damodaran. I am C. Saradambal, and I married Damodaran on 7th June 1970. We had two daughters, Prema and Deepalakshmi.

My husband was a lawyer and he survived his father by 11 years, passing away in June 1989. During all that time, he never spoke about the will or took any steps over the property. After he died, I decided to act on what I believe my father-in-law wanted. I have the original will, signed by him and witnessed by two men, Varadan and Dakshinamurthy, who were close to my husband. Dakshinamurthy has since passed away, but Varadan is alive and can confirm that the will was signed in his presence.

Now, my husband’s sisters—Savitri Ammal and Padmavathi—are saying the will is not real. They claim our father-in-law was bedridden with paralysis and could not move or write in the months before he died. They say they were the ones who cared for him and that he never mentioned making a will. They also say the two witnesses didn’t know him and were only friends of my husband. They’ve told me they believe they are entitled to a share in the house and have even asked for a division of the property.

I have documents like my father-in-law’s school certificate and a building plan with his signature. I believe those signatures match the one on the will. The will was not registered, but I truly believe it reflects his wishes. I want the house to be handled according to that will, so my children and I can have what was left to us. I want to make sure any debts or responsibilities are taken care of, and that the house is passed on as he intended.

I own a petrol service station at 4D, Council House Street, Calcutta. The land isn’t mine — it was originally leased by Abhiram Mullick (who has since passed away) to a company called Mallika Investment Company Private Limited. They allowed Dewar’s Garage India Private Limited to use the place as a monthly tenant, and Dewar’s built the station, put up the pumps, and installed all the machinery. My company, Delta International Limited, took over Dewar’s Garage when it was merged into ours.

In 1970, we made an arrangement with a company called ESSO Standard Eastern Inc. We let them use the entire petrol station — the land, the building, the pumps, everything — so they could run the business. We called it a leave and license agreement. Shyam Sunder Ganeriwalla, one of the people now in possession, started operating the station through ESSO.

We never gave them a sub-lease. In fact, we didn’t have the right to give one without written permission from our landlord, Mallika Investment Company, and we never got that. Under our deal, ESSO had to keep the equipment in working order, pay us a lump sum as advance license fee, and follow our instructions. We also had the right to end the arrangement if they didn’t follow the terms. They weren’t supposed to pay property taxes or electricity bills — we handled all that, which shows we still controlled the place.

Later, the government took over ESSO’s business and handed it to Hindustan Petroleum. But Shyam Sunder Ganeriwalla stayed on and kept running the station as if he had full rights. In May 1985, we told them the arrangement was over and asked them to leave. They refused. Since then, they’ve been using our premises and equipment without any legal right.

I want them to vacate, return everything we own, and pay me for the years they’ve been using the property — Rs. 20,000 per month from May 1, 1985. I also want a court order to stop them from using the station or anything connected to it.

My name is Govindbhai Chhotabhai Patel. I am one of the sons of Chhotabhai Ashabhai Patel, who passed away in 2001. My father had two brothers and a sister. Ramanbhai Mathurbhai Patel, the man now claiming the property, is the son of my father’s sister.

The land in question was bought long ago by my grandfather, Ashabhai Patel, with his own money. After he died, the property came to my father through a will he had made. We have a copy of that will, and the local revenue records also show that my father became the owner after my grandfather’s death, sometime in the early 1950s.

We grew up knowing this property belonged to our family. We believed it was something that would be shared among us, as his sons. But years later, we found out that in 1977, my father had supposedly signed a gift deed giving the entire property to our cousin Ramanbhai. We never saw this document when it was made, and we never heard my father mention such a gift. We only came to know about it after his death, when Ramanbhai started claiming full ownership.

We don’t believe that gift is real or valid. Even if it exists, we think our father had no right to give away this property on his own. It came from our grandfather, and it was part of our family’s heritage. We have been paying property taxes on parts of the land, and we’ve maintained our share over the years. Ramanbhai has never lived there or done any work on the property.

Now he says he owns everything because of that gift. We want to stop him from taking over and have it declared that we are rightful owners as well. We want our share in the property, and we want things set right.

Back in 1980, my father, Ayyavoo Udayar, signed an agreement to buy a piece of land in Salem from two brothers, Ramanujan and Jagadeesan. The total price was Rs 67,000. He paid Rs 10,000 right away as advance, and it was agreed that he would pay the remaining Rs 57,000 by 15 November 1980. Once they got the full amount, they were supposed to sign and register the sale deed in my father’s name.

On 15 November, my father sent them a telegram asking them to come and collect the balance. They replied saying they would do it on 20 November, but they never showed up. We kept trying to settle it through local mediators, but they refused to cooperate and even started saying they wouldn’t sell the land at all. Around that time, they got their sister’s sons—Rajamani and another man—into the property, as if they were the real occupants, even though they had no ownership.

So my father had no choice but to take legal action in 1983 to enforce the agreement. He included Rajamani and the other man in the case so that once the sale went through, there wouldn’t be any problem taking possession. They never responded or showed up during the process.

Eventually, we were told that we had won and that we could proceed with the sale. We paid the full Rs 67,000 in April 2004 as instructed. The people who sold the land tried to challenge this multiple times, but all their objections were rejected by the time early 2006 came around.

In August 2007, the sale deed was officially registered in our name. At first, Rajamani and the other man were named in the document just to clear any claims, but later we agreed to have their names removed since they never owned the land.

Even after all this, they are still living on the property and refusing to leave. They were only put there to create trouble and have no legal right to stay. I just want them to vacate so we can finally take peaceful possession of the land we’ve been trying to get for over 40 years.

I own a piece of land in Madukkarai Village, Coimbatore — about 12.60 acres, under Patta Nos. 147, 240, and 217. My husband and I bought it long ago, and it’s been with our family for years. In February 1990, we agreed to sell this land to a man named K.K. Rathinavel for ₹1.25 lakh. He paid us ₹25,000 as advance, and we agreed he would pay the remaining ₹1 lakh within six months, along with stamp duty. Once he paid everything, we would give him a proper sale deed and transfer the property, with no loans or claims on it.

At that time, there was a mortgage on the land for ₹6,000 in favour of someone named Janaki Amma. He knew about it, and we understood he would use part of the sale money to clear that debt. He gave us another ₹10,000 in March 1990. But after that, he didn’t pay the rest. We waited, but he never came forward with the balance. There was no word from him for months. So on 19 December 1990, I sent a legal notice asking him to pay. When he replied, he didn’t offer the money — instead, he said we should clear the mortgage first.

Then, in 1991, he went and got an order stopping us from selling the land to anyone else. But he still didn’t pay us. We cleared the mortgage ourselves in June 1992. Only after that, in June 1993 — more than three years after our agreement — did he say he wanted to enforce the sale. He didn’t even deposit the balance amount until years later, and eventually took it back.

My husband passed away during all this, and now I’m left dealing with this. I feel it’s unfair that after he failed to pay on time and waited so long, he’s now trying to take my land. I want to stop him from getting it. I just want to keep what belongs to me and be left alone.

We are a private company called Ferrodous Estates, and we wanted to build a multi-storey building in Madras. In June 1980, we signed an agreement to buy a piece of land from four people — P. Nagarathina Mudaliar and his three sons, including P. Gopirathnam and P. Lavakumar. The property is 8 grounds and 2354 square feet on Haddows Road. It originally belonged to a joint family — Mr. Nagarathina and his father — and after a partition in 1944, Mr. Nagarathina became the owner. That partition was recorded at the Sub-Registrar’s office.

At the time we made the deal, the land was mortgaged to Syndicate Bank for Rs. 5,65,000. The sellers told us they would pay off that loan and get a release from the bank. We agreed to pay Rs. 5,40,000 — Rs. 1,00,000 as advance, which we gave to their auditors, M/s Venkataraman & Co., and the remaining Rs. 4,40,000 we were to pay directly to the bank to clear the mortgage. The agreement also said they would get all necessary clearances — like income tax clearance and permission from the local authorities — at their own cost, and hand over the property with vacant possession before signing the final sale deed.

We were always ready to complete the purchase. We even offered to put the balance money in a safe place to show we meant business. But the sellers never got the required permissions. Instead, we heard they were trying to sell the same land to someone else for more money. They didn’t say anything about legal limits when we signed, and only later started claiming we couldn’t buy the full property because of a government rule about land size.

I want them to do what they promised — sign the sale deed and give us the property. We’ve waited long enough. They took our money, used part of it for a family wedding, and now they’re refusing to go through with the sale. I want them to complete the transaction as agreed.

I own agricultural land in Vasant Kunj, New Delhi — 33 bighas and 1 biswa. My family has held this land for generations. In 1961, the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) put out a public notice saying they were acquiring the land for the development of Delhi. At that time, nothing changed — we stayed on the land and continued to use it. Then in 1969, another notice came, but again, no action followed.  

Years passed. In 1983, officials came and said something about objections, but we weren’t told anything clearly or given any documents. We didn’t receive any money, and no one told us to leave. In 1992, I sold part of the land to three people through a registered sale deed. The buyers paid me and have been co-owners since then.  

In 1997, the government finally decided the amount they would pay for the land. But they didn’t give us the money. No one came to hand it over, and we were never asked to collect it. In January 2000, a group of officials came with police, took over the land, and made a record of the takeover — but they didn’t inform me or the buyers beforehand.  

Later, I found out that the DDA only deposited the compensation money in 2002 — five years after they decided the amount. The reason they didn’t pay us earlier was because they were confused about whether to pay me or the buyers. So they just kept the money and did nothing.  

Then I heard that a new law came into effect in January 2014 about land acquisition. Under its rules, if the government doesn’t pay the compensation within five years of deciding the amount, the acquisition no longer stands. Since they didn’t pay us by December 2013, and more than five years had passed since the 1997 decision, I believe the acquisition has automatically ended.  

I have the original land records, the registered sale deed, and all the government notices. The DDA has held the land for years without paying us fairly. I just want the land back because the process they started is no longer valid.

I am the head of the Indian Evangelical Lutheran Church Trust Association, and I need your help to stop a property dispute from going further. The land in question is part of a 5.05-acre plot in Loch End, Kodaikanal, which was originally bought in 1912 by American missionaries of the Lutheran Church. Over time, they transferred control of this property and others to our Trust. In 1975, we formalized this through a court process, and I was officially appointed as the trustee for these properties, including the Kodaikanal land, to manage them for religious and charitable purposes.

In 1991, my Trust entered into an agreement to sell a portion of this land—specifically 5.05 acres with 12 out of 15 buildings—to a company called Sri Bala & Co. The total sale price was Rs. 3.02 crores, and they paid an advance of Rs. 10 lakhs. We gave them partial possession at that time. However, they did not pay the remaining amount within the agreed 27-month period. Also, at that time, the Kodaikanal International School was already occupying three of the buildings as tenants, and we had ongoing legal issues with them.

In 1993, Sri Bala & Co. filed a case seeking to force us to complete the sale, but that case was dismissed in 1998 because they didn’t pay the required court fees. Nothing happened after that for many years. Then, in 2007—nine years later—they filed another suit asking for the same thing: specific performance of the 1991 sale agreement.

We objected, saying this second suit is too late and not allowed because they already had their chance and lost it. We also believe the agreement is no longer valid since they didn’t pay on time and the school’s presence made full possession impossible. They claim the limitation period was extended because of the disputes with the school, pointing to a letter from our then Secretary dated July 1991, which mentioned delays due to litigation.

I want to stop this 2007 suit from proceeding. I believe it’s barred by time and that allowing it would unfairly pressure us to sell property meant for religious work. I have the 1975 court order appointing us as trustees, the 1991 sale agreement, and records of all communications. I need you to help me protect the Trust’s rights over this land.

My name is K. Arumuga Velaiah, and I’m the grandson of Periyaiya Servai. I’m coming to you because I believe I’m entitled to a share in our family’s joint property, but my uncles — P.R. Ramasamy and P.R. Kasilingam — are not allowing me to claim it. The property is in Sathyamangalam village, and it’s ancestral land that was originally held by my great-grandfather, Marimuthu Servai. His two sons, Periyaiya Servai and Muthu Servai, were joint in this property. Periyaiya Servai had three sons: my father, Marimuthu (who is now deceased), and my uncles Ramasamy and Kasilingam. After my grandfather Periyaiya Servai passed away in 2003, I found out he had made a registered will on 26th January 1994, leaving his share of the joint family property to me. That should give me one-fourth of the total property, since each of the three sons and my father’s line were entitled to equal shares.

I also know that after my father died, his wife Poomayil (my mother) passed away too, and she had given her share to Ramasamy through a will. So, Ramasamy now claims half the property, and the other half should be split between me and Kasilingam. But when I tried to get my rightful share, Ramasamy sent me a legal notice denying my claim, saying the will is fake and that the property was already divided long ago in 1964. He says there was a partition among the three sons, and that my grandfather had no share left to give away. But I’ve seen the will — it’s registered, and it clearly names me as the beneficiary. I also have the revenue records showing the property is still under joint ownership, and no individual pattas were ever issued after 1964. My uncle Ramasamy has been paying kist for his portion, but that doesn’t prove a legal partition happened.

I want to get my one-fourth share of the property through partition and be given physical possession of it. I don’t want money — I want the land. I’m not trying to fight for more than what’s mine. I just want what my grandfather intended for me and what the law should protect.

I am Kedar Nath Yadav, and I am from the village of Gopalnagar in Singur, Hooghly district, West Bengal. I have been farming on a piece of land for as long as I can remember — about 1.5 acres. My family has been cultivating this land for generations. It’s fertile, and we grow paddy and vegetables. I have all the records showing my name in the land revenue papers, and I’ve been paying land tax regularly.

In early 2006, I started hearing rumors that the government was planning to take over large chunks of farmland in our area — around 1000 acres across several villages including mine — for some big industrial project. At first, we didn’t believe it, but then officials came, surveyed the land, and put up notices saying the land was being acquired for public purpose, specifically for a car factory. Later, we found out it was for Tata Motors.

We were never properly consulted. No one asked us if we wanted to give up our land. We depend on this land for our survival. The government said they would pay compensation, but the amount offered was very low, and many of us didn’t even get that fully. Some people were pressured into signing papers they didn’t understand.

I know the government claimed this project would bring jobs and development, but most of us haven’t seen any of that. The factory didn’t come up here in the end, and the land just sat unused for years. My land, which I’ve worked on all my life, was taken without my consent, and now I can’t even go there to farm.

I want my land back. I didn’t agree to sell it, and it wasn’t taken through any fair process. I’ve seen newspaper reports and some government documents through local activists, which show that the land was meant for a private company with special benefits — like being leased for 30 years at a very low rate. That doesn’t sound like public use to me.

I want you to help me get back what’s rightfully mine.

My name is Rajesh Mitra, and I’ve been living in Room No. 208 on the 2nd floor at 25-A Park Street, Kolkata, since I was a child. My father, S.K. Mitra, was the original tenant of this room. He passed away in 1970, and after his death, my mother Usha Mitra, my brother, and I continued living here. At that time, I was just 2 years old and my brother was 5. We’ve lived here our whole lives.  

After my father died, my mother became the tenant under the old tenancy law, and all the rent receipts from 1970 until her death in 2009 are in her name. She also gave an undertaking to the landlord that she was the tenant. But the law back then said that legal heirs who were living with the tenant at the time of death could also inherit the tenancy. So, I believe my brother and I became tenants along with her.  

My mother passed away on 3rd November 2009. After that, the new tenancy law came into force in 2001, but I understand that under this law, children of the tenant can continue as tenants for five years after the tenant’s death, provided they were living with them and don’t own any other house. We meet all those conditions. So, we should have been protected until 2014.  

But now, the landlord, Karnani Properties Limited, has filed a case saying that our tenancy ended in 2014 and we have no right to stay. They are using a statement I made in another case where I mentioned that the tenancy was in my mother’s name. That’s true, but I never said that my brother and I had no rights.  

They want us to vacate the room. This place is our home. We’ve paid all dues and lived here for over 50 years. I don’t own any other property. I just want to know if I have a right to stay or at least be given a fair chance to present my side. I don’t think I can be thrown out based on a statement taken out of context.

My name is Kavita Kanwar. I’m the younger daughter of Amarjeet Mamik, who passed away in May 2006. Before she died, she made a will on 20 May 2003, and in it, she clearly said that her share of our family home at D-179, Defence Colony, New Delhi, should go to me. The property is 325 square yards and has a ground floor, first floor, terrace, garage, and servant quarters.  

My father, Lt. Col. D.S. Mamik, had already given the ground floor to me in 2001 through a registered gift deed. He left the rest of the house — the first floor, terrace, and annexes — to my mother through his will. After he passed away in October 2002, she became the owner of those parts.  

When my mother made her will in 2003, she was living on the ground floor of the house, which was my portion. She did that because we were close and I was taking care of her. My elder sister, Pamela Mehta, who is widowed, was already living on the first floor.  

The will says that I get her entire share in the property, with two options: either build on the terrace and give my sister a flat there, or rebuild the whole house and give her the top floor, while I keep the terrace rights. It also says my brother, Prithiviraj Mamik, gets whatever money is in her bank accounts, but he does not get any part of the house. I’ve been named as the person to carry out her wishes.  

The will was signed by her in the presence of two people: Major General Manjit Ahluwalia, who is her nephew, and Urvinder Singh Kohli, a family friend. Part of the will is in her handwriting — the beginning and end — and the middle part is typed. I have a copy of this document.  

After she passed away, I tried to follow what she wanted. But my brother and sister are not accepting the will. They’re saying it’s not valid, even though she was in good health and mind when she signed it, and there were witnesses.  

I just want to do what my mother asked. I want the authorities to accept this will as her true last wish and let me move forward with it.

I’m Sarojini Devi, widow of the late Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha. I want your help to claim my rightful share in a property called Sterling Castle in Shimla, which my husband bought in 1921 but had to register in someone else’s name because of British rules. The real owner was my husband—he paid for it, and it was meant for our family. The sale deed is in the name of his friend, Dr. Tehl Singh, but in 1952, Dr. Tehl Singh signed a relinquishment deed saying he was only holding it for us and transferring the title to me and my three sons—Pratap Singh, Kharagh Singh, and Gurbaksh Singh.

After my husband died in 1942, we were living in England until 1954 when we returned to India. By then, Pratap Singh, as the eldest, was being prepared to take over as head of the family. But he began claiming that Sterling Castle was solely his, even though it was never just his. In 1957, when we tried to get our names on the municipal records in Shimla, he objected. Then, in 1962, without our consent, he sold the property to a foreign charity called the Save the Children Fund for Rs. 50,000. Later, they sold it to other people in 1970.

I filed a suit with my younger sons and the children of my third son Gurbaksh Singh, who passed away in 1963, for partition and joint possession. We also asked for mesne profits because we’ve been kept out of our share. Pratap Singh says the property became his by rule of succession, but that rule only applied to the throne and state property, not personal assets like this. He even included this house in a list of his private properties when the princely states merged with India, but that doesn’t make it his alone. In fact, in 1949, when he applied for letters of administration for my husband’s estate, he said he was the head of the family managing the estate—admitting it was a joint family property.

I have the relinquishment deed, sale documents, and other records. I just want what’s rightfully mine and my children’s—our share in the property or its value. I don’t want Pratap Singh to benefit unfairly from something that belonged to all of us.

I’m Jayaram Mudaliar, and I need your help to protect land I bought many years ago. Here’s what happened.

Back in 1958, I bought a piece of leasehold land from Munisami Mudaliar and his sons for Rs. 10,500. We signed a sale deed on 7th July 1958. Most of the payment wasn’t in cash. Instead, I adjusted money that Munisami already owed me from earlier. He had borrowed from me, and I had written agreements showing how much he owed. I also paid off some of his other debts—like Rs. 1,250 he owed to another man, and small amounts he owed to the government for buying cattle and digging a well. After all those adjustments, I only paid about Rs. 521 in actual cash.

Later, in 1960, another piece of land was sold at auction because Munisami hadn’t repaid a loan he took under a government land improvement scheme. The authorities held the auction to recover the money, and I bought that land too for Rs. 6,550. I have the sale certificate from that auction.

Now, Munisami’s brother, Ayyaswami Mudaliar, is saying these sales shouldn’t count because he had already started a case asking to divide the family property. He claims I can’t own the land since the first sale happened after he filed his case.

But I didn’t do anything wrong. The 1958 sale was to settle old debts that were already due. Munisami was managing the family property, and those debts were real and needed to be paid. The 1960 sale wasn’t even something I arranged—it was done by the government. I just bought the land openly and paid for it.

I have the sale deed, the auction certificate, the loan papers, and receipts showing the debts. I acted honestly and paid fair value. I want to keep the land I bought. I don’t think Ayyaswami should be able to undo my purchase just because of a family dispute he started. I want you to help me make sure I don’t lose what I rightfully own.

I bought a house in Reghar Pura, New Delhi, in 1979 — house numbers 3395–3397, in Block R, Gali No. 1. It was part of a plot originally leased in 1953 by the Delhi Improvement Trust to Shri Jagat Singh, who built the house. The lease clearly said the land and building could only be used for residential purposes. If that condition was broken, the lease would become void. After Jagat Singh’s death, I bought the property from his legal heirs.

When I took over, I found that two portions of the house were already rented out — one to Shri Jai Narain Sharma, who was running a watch repair shop, and another to Dr. Ms. Tara Motihar, who was operating a clinic. So the premises were being used for commercial purposes, not residential, which was a clear violation of the original lease terms. I had documents to prove this — rent receipts issued by the previous owner even described the rented parts as “shop” and “clinic.”

I needed the house back. I didn’t have another home of my own, and I wanted to demolish the old structure and rebuild it for my family’s use. Some of my dependents also needed a place to live. So in 1980, I filed petitions asking for the tenants to be evicted, saying I needed the property for my own bona fide use and that they were violating the lease by using it commercially.

The tenants fought back. They said my need wasn’t genuine, that I had other accommodation, and that the building couldn’t be demolished.
