They also claimed that since the earlier owner allowed commercial use and the government had issued a notification in December 1978 allowing some lease violations to be condoned, they had a right to stay.

The Rent Controller accepted that the tenants were using the premises for non-residential purposes, which broke the lease. But he said he couldn’t evict them because the law only allowed eviction on the grounds of the landlord’s personal need if the premises were originally let out for residential use. Since these were being used commercially, that ground didn’t apply.

I just want to be able to use my own property. I’ve been living with uncertainty for years. I want the tenants removed so I can rebuild and live there with my family.

My name is Ishani Prasad Basu. I am one of the legal heirs of late Pinaki Prosad Basu, and our family shares ownership of a property in Kolkata at 46A, Purna Chandra Mitra Lake. The property was originally inherited, and we all hold undivided shares in it. My family’s share is 54/240, while two other branches of the family each hold 93/240.

A few years ago, we all agreed to a development deal with a builder to redevelop the land. The plan was that after construction, three flats and three parking spaces would be given back to the owners. Once the building was complete, each family moved into one flat — we didn’t divide the property legally, but we each took possession of a flat based on our agreement.

My brother, who is 72 and lives alone, has been staying in Flat No. 201 since it was ready. He’s had the keys, paid for utilities, and treated it as his home. The other families knew about this and never objected at the time.

But in August 2006, without any warning, the other side — relatives from one of the other branches — came and changed the lock on Flat No. 201. They put their own things inside and said he couldn’t go back in. They even brought some men with them, which was intimidating. My brother was left out of his own home, and he’s been distressed ever since.

We went to the local court and explained what happened. We said he was already living there and they had no right to lock him out. The court heard the facts and said they had to remove the lock and their belongings and let my brother live in peace.

Now they are trying to challenge that decision, but the truth is simple: they took action on their own, without any legal process, and removed someone from a place he was already living. I just want my brother to be able to stay in the flat without fear or interference. We’re not asking for full ownership yet — only that no one should be allowed to take the law into their own hands and throw us out like this.

I am the son of Devi Prasad Khanna, and my family has been connected to a property at 21, Aurangzeb Road, New Delhi for many decades. The land was originally given on lease by the British government to my grandfather, Sidh Nath Khanna, in the 1930s. After a family division in 1955, this property came to my father. When he passed away, my name was officially recorded in the government land records in 1977 as the person in charge of the lease.

Since 1962, the Sudan Embassy had been using the property as a residence. They left in May 1992, and after that, I took possession. I handed it over to a person who was helping me with plans to redevelop the site.

Back in September 1988, I had signed an agreement to sell this property to a company called Tosh Apartments Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 2.5 crores. This was a real sale deal, not a loan or anything else. Around the same time, I had also taken some loans and mortgaged the property to a few people — first to S.N. Tondon in 1980, then to Avtar Singh in 1987, and later to another party. I also had a short-lived development agreement with someone else, but we cancelled it.

In 1997, I entered into agreements to sell the property to six companies — Vidur Impex and others — for Rs. 2.88 crores, and the sale documents were registered that year. These buyers then made their own deal with another company, Bhagwati Developers, and took an advance of Rs. 3.05 crores from them.

Later, I came to know that Tosh Apartments had started some legal process claiming that I had agreed to sell the property to them first and should not have sold it to anyone else. They say I was not supposed to transfer the property after 1988. They also say that the new buyers cannot claim ownership because of that earlier agreement.

I have the 1988 agreement, the lease records, and all the government entries showing my connection to the property. I want to make sure that my rights under that 1988 sale are respected. I don’t want these other parties taking control of the land based on deals made after I was already committed to Tosh Apartments. I want to stop them from claiming the property or trying to take possession.

My name is Meenakshi Ammal. I want to tell you about a piece of land and the cinema theatre my family has been running for years. My husband, Kannaiya Chettiar, took a lease of this land along with another man in 1953 from a man named Sethurama Chettiar. The rent was Rs.150 per month, and they had it for 12 years. We built a cinema theatre called Raja Talkies on that land at our own expense, and it’s still there today.

After the other partner passed away, my husband became the sole person managing the theatre. Then, in 1967, he signed a new lease agreement with the Gangai Vinayagar Temple Trust—Sethurama Chettiar was the head of it—for 15 years starting from 1968. After my husband died, I continued living and working there with my children, and we’ve been treating this place as our livelihood.

In 1976, we were told that the Trust had sold the land to three men—P. Lakshmanan, P. Vadivelu, and P. Saibabha—and that we now had to pay rent to them. We were shocked because we believed that since the land belonged to a religious trust, the sale needed official permission, which we don’t think was ever obtained. We were afraid they would try to remove us, so we went to court to stop them from taking over, saying the sale wasn’t valid.

At the same time, the Trust started asking for unpaid rent from earlier years. Three separate cases came up—one from us, and two from them over rent. All were dealt with together, and eventually, the court said we couldn’t challenge the ownership of the people who bought the land and that we had to accept them as the new landlords.

We didn’t go back to court to question that decision at the time. But now, they’re using that old outcome to say we can never question their right to the land. I feel that wasn’t fair because we never got a proper chance to prove that the sale was illegal. The theatre is our life. I want to make sure we’re not thrown out and that we can keep running Raja Talkies without fear. I want to challenge the sale and protect our right to stay.

I am a member of the Balco Employees Union, and I’m speaking on behalf of the workers who have spent years building Bharat Aluminium Company Limited (BALCO) into what it is today. BALCO was set up in 1965 as a government company, and over the years, the government invested heavily in it. It has major plants in Korba, Chhattisgarh, and another in West Bengal. The land for these plants was given by the state governments—some on lease, and some acquired from private owners with compensation paid. We’ve been working there for decades, and our lives are tied to this company.

Since the 1990s, there’s been talk about selling off government companies, and now the government wants to sell 51% of BALCO’s shares and hand over management control to a private buyer. This decision was made without properly consulting us or protecting our jobs. We were told that the Disinvestment Commission, set up in 1996, recommended selling a big chunk of shares, and later, they even suggested increasing it to 51% or more. A global advisor, Jardine Fleming, was hired in 1999 to handle the sale, and in 2000, they invited expressions of interest from private companies, including Sterlite and others.

We found out that the government reduced BALCO’s share capital from Rs. 488.85 crores to half, which brought in a huge amount of money to the government. That felt like they were dismantling the company piece by piece. The whole process seems rushed and secretive. We don’t know who will buy the company, what will happen to our jobs, or whether the new owners will respect the working conditions we’ve fought for.

We’re not against change, but we can’t accept being left out of decisions that affect our livelihoods. We want the government to stop this sale, protect our rights as employees, and ensure that whatever happens, our jobs, benefits, and the public nature of this company are safeguarded. We need your help to challenge this before it’s too late.

Back in November 2011, I paid Rs 3.5 lakh to a company called Jai Prakash Associates for a flat in a housing project they were building in Noida called KRESCENT Homes. The flat was supposed to be around 114 square metres, and the total price was Rs 56.45 lakh. They gave me a letter saying I was provisionally allotted the unit, and we agreed I’d get possession within 42 months.  

From December 2011 onwards, I kept paying them as per their demands. Over the years, I’ve paid Rs 53.84 lakh—almost the full amount. But they never completed the project, and I never got the flat. I’ve been following up for years, but nothing changed.  

In June 2017, I wrote to them asking for a refund of the money I’d paid, along with 18% interest, since they hadn’t delivered. I didn’t get any proper response. I wrote again in April 2020, same thing—no reply. So in June 2020, I filed a complaint with the national consumer body in Delhi, asking them to order the company to return my money with interest.  

But a few weeks later, I was told that because of a new rule that came into effect in July 2020, the body can no longer hear cases like mine unless the amount involved is over Rs 10 crore. My claim, including interest, is about Rs 2.19 crore, so they said they can’t take it up. They dismissed my case. I asked them to reconsider, but they refused.  

What bothers me is that I filed my case before the new rule came into force. I acted in time. I’ve heard others who filed around the same date are still being heard. I’ve lost a huge amount of money and time. I just want to get back what I paid, with fair interest. I need help to make sure my case is heard by the right authority.

I need your help because a society is trying to take away the land I’ve been living on for most of my life. The property is in Tiruvannamalai, part of T.S. No. 1646/1, about 70 feet by 30 feet, with Old Door No. 116 and New Door No. 65. It was originally set aside long ago for a dharamshala — a place where people from the Ariya Kshatriya community could stay — but nothing was ever built on this portion.

My father, Appadurai Pillai, worked as a watchman for the society that manages this land. Because of that job, he was allowed to live on this small piece of land. He started staying here in the 1940s, and after he passed away, I continued living here. I’ve been here for decades, treating it as my home. I’ve maintained the place, paid house tax every year since at least 2000, and have receipts to show it.

In 1994, the society suddenly claimed full ownership and tried to remove me by force. I got scared and filed a case asking to be left alone, but I lost that case. Then, in 2003, they filed another case and got an order saying I have to give up the land. I didn’t move because I believe I’ve been here long enough, openly and without anyone’s permission, to have a right to it.

I have documents that show my connection to the place — tax receipts, the society’s own records, maps, and even old applications they made to the local authorities. I also have copies of their bylaws and registration papers. I’ve lived here with my family, not as a servant or guest, but as someone who treats this land as his own.

They say I’m just the son of a watchman who stayed here by permission, but that’s not true anymore. I’ve been here too long, on my own terms. I don’t want to be thrown out of my home. I want to stop them from removing me and prove that I have the right to stay.

I own a piece of land in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh. It’s part of a larger area known as Government Burial Poramboke, and my portion is officially recorded as S.No. 35/5, later renumbered as 35/5-C1/A-1. I’ve been in possession of this land for many years. On June 1, 1982, I signed a lease deed with a man named Haji Mian, allowing him to use the land as a tenant for three years at a monthly rent of Rs. 150. That was the agreement—we both signed it.

After the three years ended, he didn’t leave. Instead, without my permission, he built four huts on the land and started renting them out to other people. He stopped paying me any rent and began saying that he and his family actually owned the land. When Haji Mian passed away, his family—his mother, wife, sons, and daughters—stayed on the land and kept making the same claim.

I’ve tried to get them off the property and also want to recover money for the time they’ve used it without paying. From July 1989 to July 1992, that’s 36 months, I’m claiming Rs. 5,400, plus Rs. 150 per month for the earlier period when they were supposed to be paying. I filed two cases—one for eviction and one for the money owed.

On their side, Haji Mian’s family also started legal action. They filed three cases claiming they’ve been in possession of the land for over 100 years, even before I came into the picture, and say that because of that long stay, they now own it. They also challenged the electricity connection to the huts and objected to my name being listed in the municipal records for the property.

All these cases are about the same piece of land and involve the same people, so they’ve been grouped together. I have the original lease deed from 1982, and I’ve been paying taxes and keeping records under my name. Their claim is based only on their family’s long stay, but I never gave up my rights or agreed to transfer ownership.

I just want to be recognized as the rightful owner and get them removed from my land. I need help stopping their false claims and protecting what is legally mine.

I have been running my business from a small shop – Shop No. SF-2 – on the second floor of Omaxe Square in Jasola, New Delhi. The shop is about 317 square feet. I took it on a three-year lease back in 2010 from the previous owner. The agreement was in writing and had a clause stating that if any dispute comes up between us, it should be settled through arbitration. I moved in and started using the shop for my business.

That original lease period ended in 2013, but I continued to stay and run my business there. I kept paying rent every month, and the current owner, Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia, accepted it without any objection. So things went on as before, just on a month-to-month basis.

In August 2015, he suddenly filed a case against me. I got notice of it. He wants me to be thrown out of the shop, says I owe some unpaid rent, and wants a permanent order stopping me from using the place. When I learned about this, I asked the court to stop the case and instead send the matter to arbitration, because that’s what we had agreed in the original lease.

He is now saying that since the original lease term is over, the agreement no longer applies, so the arbitration clause doesn’t bind him. He also claims that disputes about eviction and rent can’t be handled through arbitration anyway.

But I’ve been there continuously, paying rent regularly, and the relationship between us still comes from that original lease. I have the lease document and all my rent receipts. I just want things to follow the agreement we both signed. I don’t think he can ignore the arbitration clause now just because he wants to take the matter to court. I want the dispute to be settled through arbitration as we had agreed, not through this case.

I own a house in New Friends Colony, Delhi. It’s a residential property I had built recently — it has a dining room, drawing room, three bedrooms with attached bathrooms, a study, a family lounge, and a garage. When the construction was finished, I didn’t need to move into it right away because my father was living alone and in poor health. My mother had passed away, and I was staying with him at 4-Flag Staff Road to take care of him, so I wasn’t using this new house for myself or my family.

Around mid-1976, I decided to let the house out for a fixed period of two years. I found someone who agreed to rent it only for that time, and we both went to the Rent Controller’s office together. I told them clearly that I didn’t need the house for the next two years and that I was letting it out only for that limited period, for residential use. The person renting it also said on record that he understood and would leave after two years. The Rent Controller allowed the arrangement.

When the two years ended in July 1978, I asked him to vacate, but he refused. He’s still living there even though he agreed upfront that his stay was temporary. I now need the house for myself and my family, especially since my father has passed away and I no longer have to stay elsewhere. I have the site plan of the property and a copy of the written agreement we submitted at the time. I just want to get back possession of my own home, which was only ever meant to be rented out for a short time. He agreed to that, and I expect him to keep his word.

My grandfather, Bishan Sahai Vidyarthi, made a will on 21 November 1965. He had five sons—Rameshwar, Rajeshwar, Harbansh, Raghuvansh, and Krishan Sahai. My father was Harbansh Sahai, and I am his son, Narendra Gopal Vidyarthi. Rajat Vidyarthi, who is now claiming rights over the property, is the son of Rameshwar Sahai, the youngest of the five brothers.

Within a month of making the will, a house was bought for Rs. 32,000. Part of that money came from funds my grandfather had set aside for my mother, Chandramukhi, and me under the will. My grandfather passed away around 1973. After that, the local revenue records were changed to show my mother and me as the owners of the property. No one in the family raised any objection at the time.

For many years, the family treated the house as belonging to my mother and me. There were no disputes. But much later, Rajat started saying the house is joint family property and that I have no right to it. He says I shouldn’t be able to manage or decide anything about the house. I have the will, and I know the money used to buy the house came from the portion meant for us under that will. I also have the revenue records showing our names as owners, updated soon after my grandfather’s death.

I don’t understand how it can be called joint family property when it was bought with money set aside for my mother and me, and when the records were changed without any objection from the rest of the family for so many years. I want to make sure that it’s recognized as our property, not something the whole family can claim. I want to be able to protect our rights over the house and stop any claim that it belongs to everyone.

My name is Ramachandra Reddy, and I am the daughter of Venkata Reddy, one of three brothers—Venkatarama Reddy, Venkata Reddy (also known as Pakki Reddy), and Chenga Reddy. They all lived together and shared the land their father, Balu Reddy, left behind. Each brother had an equal share in the property. My father passed away, and I am his only legal heir. Venkatarama Reddy had a son named Markandeya Reddy, and Chenga Reddy had no children.

In 1963, my father and Chenga Reddy signed a document in favour of Govindammal, who was married to my brother. The document says they gave her a two-thirds share in the family land because she took care of them and would continue to do so. It mentions a payment of Rs. 5,000 and lists several pieces of land—survey numbers 176, 221, 201, 163, and 160—in villages like Amambakkam, Seethanperi, and Ramanathapuram. The total land involved is around 17 to 18 acres, some dry and some wet.

For years, Govindammal kept that original document and claimed a larger share. In 1986, she took it to the revenue office to update the records, but nothing was officially changed, and she never returned the deed.

But in 1984, before all that, the village panchayat sat with both sides and decided the land should be split equally—half for us and half for Markandeya Reddy’s family. Since then, we’ve been farming our half separately. We have our own patta, we pay our own taxes, and the revenue records show our names for our portion. We’ve been in full possession of our half for decades.

Now, Markandeya Reddy’s side is saying they are entitled to two-thirds of the land based on that 1963 document. But that doesn’t reflect what actually happened on the ground. The family agreed to an equal split, and we’ve been living by it. I want the authorities to recognize our 50% share and give us clear rights over the land we’ve been cultivating all these years. I don’t want them to take more than half based on a document that was set aside by the family’s own agreement.

I own a piece of agricultural land in Delhi, about two acres, which has been with my family for as long as anyone remembers. My grandfather worked on it, then my father, and I’ve been managing it for years. We’ve always paid the land taxes, and the revenue records show us as the owners. The land is near what is now a developed area, but back when this started, it was all farmland.

Sometime in the early 1960s, maybe 1962 or 1963, I remember officials putting up a notice or something saying the government wanted to acquire our land and many others around it for city development. They said it was for building proper colonies, roads, and housing because so many people were coming to Delhi. But after that notice, nothing happened for years. No one came to take the land, no money was offered, and we just kept using it like before.

We heard the government had made some kind of plan for Delhi, and our land was included in it. But even though they said they were acquiring it, they didn’t do anything for nearly 15 or 16 years. Then, suddenly in 1979 or 1980, they issued a compensation amount. When we saw it, we were shocked—it was based on land prices from the 1960s, when the first notice came. By the time they actually started taking possession, land in that area was worth many times more. We got only a small fraction of what it was really worth.

Some of us had even sent formal letters asking the government to either acquire the land or leave it alone, and there was supposed to be a rule that if they didn’t act within six months, the acquisition would lapse. But they ignored that and still claimed the land.

I don’t understand how it’s fair to freeze the value of our land for two decades while the city grows around it. We didn’t stop them—we waited, thinking the process would move. Now I want to be paid what the land was worth when they actually took it, not from 20 years earlier. That’s all I’m asking—fair value for what they took.

I’m Maya Devi, and I need your help to protect my home in Delhi. Back in 2006, I bought a piece of land with a house on it from a woman named Nirmal Verma. She gave me a registered General Power of Attorney on May 12, 2006, for Rs. 70,000, which I paid in full, in cash. The document was registered, and she signed it in front of the Sub-Registrar. On that same day, she handed over the keys and I moved in. Since then, I’ve been living there, paying all the bills, and treating it as my own.

Now, a man named Lalta Prasad is trying to take this property from me. He says he had some kind of agreement with Nirmal Verma’s husband, Prem Chand Verma, back in 2003. But I never knew about this, and nothing was ever shown to me. Prem Chand Verma never lived here, never managed the property, and didn’t stop Nirmal Verma from selling it to me. She was the one who gave me the document and possession.

What’s more, this man Lalta Prasad never came forward when I took possession. He only showed up years later, saying he’s owed money and wants to sell the property to recover it. But he doesn’t have a registered sale agreement—just an unregistered paper, and he claims he paid everything in cash with no proper receipts.

I have a registered document, I’ve been in the house for years, and I paid for it fairly. Nirmal Verma dealt with me directly, and I’ve done nothing wrong. Now I’m being told someone else can take my home based on a deal no one ever saw and that wasn’t even registered.

I want to stop him from taking my property. I want to be recognized as the rightful owner and to live in peace without anyone threatening to throw me out. This is my home, and I want it protected.

I am an old man now, and I’ve been living on this piece of land for over sixty years. The property is 2 acres and 61 cents in Survey No.845/1, in Thimmanayakanur village, Andipatti Taluk, Madurai District. My family’s connection to it goes back a long time. My grandfather, Irulappan, gave a loan to Vellaiya Thevar, and when he couldn’t repay, his sons—Thavasi, Kuruppa, Subbaiah and Sangu Thevar—sold the land to my father, Puliyankaladi, in 1928. That sale was properly registered.

Later, my father mortgaged the land to Veluchamy and Vellamal. On 31st May 1961, he took another loan from them, also by mortgage. I paid off both of those loans on 24th June 1963. Then, on 15th July 1963, I bought the entire property from my father and his family—Irulan, Balakrishnan, and his two minor children, Senthilkumaran and Backialakshmi—through a registered sale deed. Since then, I’ve been in full possession. I got the government records changed to show my name, received the patta, and have been paying the land tax regularly all these years.

The people now troubling me are my neighbours. One lives on the north side, the other on the south. They are not related to me or to my family. They started asking me to sell them the land. When I said no, they became angry and began creating problems. On 5th June 1994, they came with a group of people trying to enter my land, but some fellow villagers helped me stop them.

Now they are saying part of my land belongs to them. One says her parents owned 75 cents and mortgaged it in 1961. The other claims she bought 30 cents in 1974, including a well and some water channels. But I have no knowledge of any of that, and I’ve never accepted their claims.

I want to be left in peace on my land. I want someone to confirm that this land is mine and stop them from coming onto it or disturbing me. I’ve lived here all this time, paid for it, and taken care of it. It’s mine by right.

I live on Gopal Doctor Road in Kolkata and have been a resident here for over twenty years. I own a house on this road, and it’s been my home for a long time. A plot next to me, numbered 8/1F, belongs to a man named Sarjun Prasad Shaw. He gave the land to a builder, Mohammad Shahid of Unique Construction, to develop. Many years ago, in 1990, the local authorities approved a plan for a two-storey building on that plot, with five years to complete it. But nothing was built back then.

Almost two decades later, in 2009, construction suddenly started. Instead of following the old approved plan, they began putting up a much taller building. I saw them erecting strong concrete columns going up to the third floor, along with a staircase, clearly going beyond what was allowed. The local building department came and issued a notice to stop work, but the builder didn’t stop. They kept going and even added a fourth floor.

Later, officials inspected the site and said the structure was unsafe and could be dangerous to people living nearby. In early 2010, they demolished about 600 square feet of the illegal portion, but left the rest standing. Since then, the builder has continued working and nearly completed the whole building, even though it’s not built according to the original permission.

This unauthorised construction is right beside my house. It blocks sunlight and airflow, increases noise and traffic, and I’m worried the building might not be safe. If something goes wrong, my family and I are at risk. I’ve seen how other illegal structures in poor areas get removed quickly, but this one remains, even though it’s much bigger and more dangerous.

I want the entire part of the building that was built without approval — everything beyond the original two-storey plan — to be completely removed. It’s not fair that some people can ignore the rules and nothing is done, while ordinary residents suffer. I just want to live in peace, in a safe and healthy environment, like everyone else.

I run a small steel business called Devi Ispat Ltd. A few years ago, we signed a contract with the zonal office of the Central Bank of India for a financial arrangement to support our operations. The contract was properly executed, and we’ve been meeting all our obligations on time. There’s a clause in the agreement that says if any dispute comes up, it should be settled through arbitration. We agreed to that, and so did they.

Recently, without warning or explanation, the bank suddenly froze a key facility we depend on. This wasn’t a minor issue — it’s directly affecting our ability to operate. Orders are getting delayed, workers are at risk of not getting paid, and suppliers are pulling back. We’ve tried to talk to them, sent emails, letters, even went to their office, but they’re not responding. No reason, no discussion — just silence.

We know the contract says disputes go to arbitration, and we’re not against that in principle. But the process takes time, and we can’t wait months while our business collapses. What they’re doing feels unfair — not just a normal business disagreement. They’re a big public institution, and they’re acting like they don’t have to answer to anyone. It’s not just about money; it’s about being treated fairly.

We have the original contract, all our payment receipts, and every piece of communication we’ve sent trying to resolve this. We just want someone to step in and stop them from doing this to us until things can be sorted out properly. We need protection now, so we don’t lose everything we’ve built.

My name is Vidya Devi. I’m telling you about a piece of land in Macangir village, Delhi, in khasra numbers 2, 5/1 and 6/1. It belonged to my father-in-law, Raghunath. When he died in 1952, I, his son Dev Raj, and his younger son Prem Prakash became the legal heirs. I am the widow of his eldest son, Ram Narain, who died before him. In 1953–54, during the jamabandi, the revenue records were updated to show our names—mine, Dev Raj’s, and Prem Prakash’s—as joint holders of the land.

Later, in 1958, a formal declaration was made under the Delhi Land Reforms rules that we were all co-owners of the land, each with a one-third share. That’s when we officially became bhumidars. The land has never been divided among us.

In October 1973, I filed a case before the Revenue Assistant asking for a partition of my one-third share and to be given physical possession of it. Dev Raj agreed—he also wanted his share and had no problem with the partition. But Prem Prakash objected. He said he has been in sole possession of the land since 1953–54 and claims that because of this long possession, the entire land now belongs only to him. He says no one else has any right over it.

I don’t accept this. We were all named together as owners in the records. I didn’t give up my share, and I never agreed to let him keep everything. There was no document, no agreement, nothing that says I lost my right. The Revenue Assistant looked at his claim and said it wasn’t a real dispute over ownership—just an excuse to avoid giving me my share. That decision was later supported by a higher revenue authority.

But Prem Prakash challenged that too and got a hearing from a higher body, which said his claim should be treated as a title dispute and sent to a civil court. That’s why I’m here. I just want my one-third share of the land to be separated and handed over to me. I’m not asking for more. I want what rightfully belongs to me.

I run a cement manufacturing company, and we’ve been operating in Tamil Nadu for years. Back in 1963, the state government gave us a mining lease for 133.91 acres of land in Chinnagoundanur, Salem district, to extract limestone and kankar for our factory. Most of that land—126.14 acres—was private patta land, and the rest, 7.77 acres, was government land. The lease was granted under the Mineral Concession Rules, and we’ve been paying all the required amounts since then: royalty, dead rent, surface rent, everything. The royalty rates were clearly set—like 75 paise per tonne on government land for limestone, with rebates if we used certain processing methods.

But in 1964, the state amended the Madras Panchayats Act and suddenly started treating royalty as part of “land revenue.” Because of that, they began demanding a local cess—45 paise for every rupee of land revenue, which now included our royalty. That’s a huge additional cost, and it was applied retroactively. In April 1965, the Collector sent us a notice saying we owed this cess for mining done since July 1961, and threatened serious consequences if we didn’t pay.

We’ve always paid what we’re supposed to under the lease. But this new demand treats royalty—money we pay for mineral rights—as if it were land revenue, just so the local panchayat can slap a tax on it. The state says it’s allowed because of an old law, but this royalty is governed by central rules under the Mines and Minerals Act, and it was never meant to be treated like land tax. We believe this cess is unfair and beyond what the state can legally impose.

I want to stop this demand. I don’t want to pay a tax that’s being wrongly applied to our royalty payments. We’ve followed all the rules, and this extra charge is unjust. I need your help to challenge this and make sure we’re not forced to pay something that shouldn’t apply to us.

We are a group of families who have owned forest land in Kerala for many years. The land has been with us since before 1971, and we have documents showing our ownership. It’s located in a rural area, and we’ve used it for timber, farming, and other traditional purposes.  

In 1971, the government announced it would take over all private forests in the state and give them to landless farmers and agricultural workers. Our land was included in this takeover, even though we were using it and had legal rights over it. We didn’t agree with this, so we went to the local court to challenge it. In December 1982, the court ruled in our favour and said the government couldn’t take our land the way it had planned.  

After that, the government went to the higher court in Delhi, but in July 1983, that court refused to hear their challenge. They didn’t give any reasons — they just said they wouldn’t take up the case. We understood this to mean the 1982 decision stood, and we were safe.  

But in January 1984, the government went back to the same court in Kerala and asked them to re-examine their 1982 decision. We objected, saying they couldn’t do that after the higher court had already stepped in. But in December 1995, the court said the government could go ahead and try to change the earlier order.  

We don’t understand how a decision that was already looked at by the higher court can be reopened. It feels like there’s no finality. We want someone to tell us that once the higher court refuses to hear a challenge, the earlier decision should be final and can’t be changed. That’s what we’re asking for — fairness and protection of our land rights.

I am one of the Podhu Dikshitars, a group of Smarthi Brahmins whose families have lived in Chidambaram for generations. We have been managing the Sri Sabhanayagar Temple, dedicated to Lord Natraja, since long before any of us can remember. Our ancestors were called to establish and serve this temple, and we’ve continued that responsibility—performing rituals, maintaining the premises, and looking after all its lands and assets. We’ve always treated the temple and its property as ours to manage as part of our religious tradition.

In 1951, the state government issued a notice saying the temple would now be under new rules, and they appointed an outside officer to run it. My elders and others at the time challenged that move, and eventually, the government stepped back and removed that officer.

Then in 1987, the same thing happened again—the Commissioner of Religious Endowments appointed another outside officer to take over the management of the temple. We objected strongly. We went through the required steps, including filing a revision petition, but in 2006, the government said the officer could continue because the law allowed it. They said the officer was only there to manage the property in a fair and orderly way, not to remove us completely. But in practice, we’ve been left out. Since 1997, this officer has been in charge, making decisions about temple lands, finances, and daily operations without our involvement.

They’ve said we didn’t maintain proper records, but that doesn’t erase the fact that we’ve been the ones caring for this temple for centuries. We’re not against proper management, but we believe we have the right to be the ones managing our own religious institution.

I want the officer’s control to end. I want us, the Podhu Dikshitars, to be restored as the rightful managers of the Sri Sabhanayagar Temple and its properties, as we have been for generations.

I am P. Kannadasan, and I have been mining granite in Tamil Nadu for many years. I lease the land where the mining happens, and I’ve been paying various charges to the local authorities. One of these charges has been a percentage they take based on the land revenue, but they also included the royalty and lease payments I make to the government as part of that calculation. I didn’t question it at the time — it was demanded every year, and I paid it like everyone else to avoid trouble.

Over the years, I paid a significant amount of money under this charge. But later, I came to know that a court had said this kind of charge was not something the local government was allowed to collect, because mining and minerals are under the control of the central government, not the local or state authorities. After that, some people stopped paying, and there was talk that those of us who had already paid could ask for our money back.

But then, in early 1992, I heard that the central government passed a new rule that made all those past collections legal after the fact. It said that even if the charge wasn’t valid before, it would now be treated as if it had always been valid, and no one could go to court to get a refund. This was done to help state governments keep the money they had collected.

I feel this is wrong. I paid money for years under a charge that was later found to be beyond the authority of the local body. Now, a new rule has been made that blocks me from getting that money back. I didn’t do anything wrong — I just followed what I was told to do. I want to challenge this because I believe I should have the right to claim back what was taken from me under a charge that wasn’t lawful. I want the chance to get what’s fair.

I am Dev Sharan, and I live in village Murchha, tehsil Puwayan, district Shahjahanpur, Uttar Pradesh. I am a bhumidar, and I’ve been farming my land here for years. The land has been in our family for generations, and it’s fertile agricultural land—good for growing crops. I own a portion of a bigger plot that the government now wants to take from us. The total area they are acquiring is about 25.89 hectares, spread across our village, and my land is part of it.

In August 2008, I came to know that the state government had issued a notification saying they were acquiring this land to build a new district jail. The old jail is in the middle of Shahjahanpur city, crowded and old, built back in 1870, and they say they need to shift it outside the city. But what they don’t say is that there are other, unused lands—banjar land—that could be used instead. My land and the lands of my neighbours are productive, well-cultivated, and we depend on them for our livelihood.

What bothers me most is that they skipped a key step: they didn’t hold the hearing that landowners are supposed to have under the law. Normally, after the first notice, there’s a process where we can go and raise objections, speak up if we think the acquisition is wrong or unfair. But they said it was an “urgent” case and just cancelled that hearing. How can it be urgent when they’ve been talking about moving the jail since at least 2004? They formed committees, held meetings in 2005 and again in 2007, and only in 2008 did they move to acquire our land. There was plenty of time to follow the rules.

I have my land records, patta, and revenue documents showing my ownership and cultivation. I’ve paid all dues and taxes. I don’t want to stop the jail from being built, but not at the cost of our livelihoods when other land is available. I want the government to reconsider the site and not take our farmland. If they must take land, let it be the unused, barren land—not ours.

I own a piece of land in Kalappanaickenpatti village, Survey No. 172/1, measuring 1,777 and a half square feet. I bought it on July 16, 2001, through a registered sale deed from the legal heirs of a man named Dhasi Naidu. He had gone to Sri Lanka many years ago as a farm labourer and died there. His son Krishnasamy Naidu came back to India in 1981 and gave someone named Ghani Sahib the responsibility to manage the property. The family later decided to sell it, and I purchased it for a fair price. I have the registered sale deed, and along with it, a power of attorney signed by the legal heirs in Sri Lanka on May 22, 2001, which was later registered in Namakkal. I also have a house tax receipt from February 2001 in my name.

After buying the property, I took possession. I even tore down the old structure that was there to start building something new. Since then, I’ve been in full and peaceful control of the land. But the first man, a retired soldier, and his son-in-law, who works as a police constable, started causing problems. They say they have a right to the land because Dhasi Naidu’s son Sanjeevi Naidu gave power of attorney to another man, P. Rangaraju Naidu, and that they are the rightful heirs through that line.

Years ago, this same man filed a case claiming ownership and possession of the same property, saying Ghani Sahib had no right to manage it. But that case was dismissed. The people handling that case also said in their records that Ghani Sahib was in possession, and they didn’t challenge that fact. Now they’re trying to stop me, even though I bought the property legally and have been on it without any issues until they started interfering.

I just want to be able to use my land without fear or harassment. I have the documents showing I bought it fairly, and I’ve been on it openly. I want you to help me stop them from coming onto my land or threatening me in any way. I want peace and protection over what I own.

My name is P. Sellathal, and I am the wife of the late M.C. Kallikutty. We owned two plots of land in Sanganur Village, Survey Nos. 472 and 488. In 1995, a poultry business called Coimbatore Hatcheries took a loan of Rs.49.5 lakhs from Canara Bank. The bank says my husband stood as a guarantor and mortgaged our land by giving the title documents to the bank. But he never signed any guarantee, and we never received any money from the loan. We had no idea about this arrangement.

Years passed, and in 2001, the bank started recovery action because the business failed to repay. They claimed my husband had given his property as security. In 2003, they got an order allowing them to recover the full amount — over Rs.57 lakh with 18% interest — from our land. In 2007, they sold some other assets of the business and recovered about Rs.38 lakhs, but still wanted to take our land for the balance.

When my husband learned about this, he went to the police and said the documents were forged. He never signed anything. Based on his complaint, an FIR was registered in 2005. The police investigated and filed a chargesheet in 2007, accusing the owners of the poultry business and even a bank officer of fraud and forgery. Later, the criminal court found the two business owners guilty of forging documents, including a property deed in my husband’s name, by faking signatures and thumbprints.

By then, we had already sold the two plots to new buyers who are now living on the land. These buyers found out the bank was trying to seize the property and filed legal cases to protect themselves. They say they bought the land in good faith and should not lose it because of a fake loan deal they knew nothing about. They want to stop the bank from taking any action against the land — no attachment, no sale.

The bank is now trying to block these cases, saying only a special debt body can hear such matters. But I believe this is a clear case of fraud. We never agreed to any mortgage. I want the court to protect the buyers and declare that the bank has no right over our land.

I own a small shop, Shop No. 408, in Pandit Lila Ram Market, Masjid Moth, New Delhi. I’ve had this shop for many years—it’s my property, and I’ve been getting it rented out to earn some income. In 1980, I gave it on rent to Mr. Vasdev. He started paying rent regularly at first, but from January 1980, he stopped paying. No rent came from him for over a year.  

In May 1981, I sent him a formal notice asking him to clear the arrears of rent within two months, as required by law. He didn’t pay anything. So in August 1982, I filed a case to get the shop back because he hadn’t paid. The Rent Controller looked into it and, in January 1984, passed an order saying that Vasdev had to pay all the back rent—Rs. 50 per month from January 1980—within one month. He also had to keep paying the monthly rent on time from then on, by the 15th of each month.  

After that order, he paid me only Rs. 500 and promised to clear the rest soon. But he didn’t. He missed the deadline and didn’t pay the full amount. So in April 1984, I went back to the Rent Controller and asked that his defence be struck out since he had failed to follow the order. The Controller then passed an eviction order in my favour, saying Vasdev had lost his right to stay because he didn’t comply.  

But later, somehow, the matter was re-examined, and they said there was a compromise or that the delay wasn’t serious. They allowed him to stay, saying he could still get protection under the law. I don’t understand how this can happen—he didn’t pay as ordered, and now he’s still occupying my shop. I’ve not received proper rent for years. I want to get my shop back and remove him. I need your help to make sure he doesn’t get away with this.

My name is Kedar Nath, and I’m the grandson of Rai Sahib Kedar Nath, who started several schools in Delhi between 1912 and 1916 in memory of his father, Lala Ramjas Mal. He bought about 1800 bighas of land in two villages—Chowkri Mubarikabad and Sadhora Khurd—which are now part of Delhi. He used his own money and donations from others to buy this land. In 1916, at a public event in one of the schools, he announced that he was dedicating all his movable and immovable property, including this land, for the purpose of promoting education, especially for poor students. He formed the Ramjas College Society in 1917 under the Societies Registration Act, and its main goals were running schools and colleges, training teachers, and supporting education without any religious bias. He was the president of the managing committee.

In 1936, he formally transferred the entire land to the Society through a release deed. Later, in 1967, the Society was renamed Ramjas Foundation and re-registered under that name.

Now, the issue is this: in 1959, the government issued a notification saying it wanted to acquire large tracts of land in Delhi for planned development. But that notification clearly said that land attached to religious institutions, graveyards, shrines, and Wakf property would not be acquired. My grandfather dedicated this land for charitable educational purposes, and we’ve always treated it as such. The Society has been running 19 schools, a degree college, and even a sports institute on parts of this land.

But despite the exemption, the government went ahead and included our 872 bighas in Chowkri Mubarikabad and 730 bighas in Sadhora Khurd in the acquisition. We objected through a lawyer at the time, but our objections were rejected. Over the years, the area has developed—some parts are now residential colonies, others industrial—but our land was taken without proper recognition of its status.

I want the land back, or at least to be treated fairly. If the government recognized that Wakf and religious land should be excluded, and my grandfather dedicated this land for a permanent charitable purpose, then it should qualify for that exemption. We’ve been running educational institutions for over a century. This land was never meant for personal gain—it was given for the public good. I want you to help us claim what’s rightfully ours based on that original dedication.

My name is Raj Kumari, and I’m the daughter of Harbans Lal and Suhagwanti Devi. My family came to Delhi during Partition in 1947. My father applied for a two-room house in Gur Mandi, Civil Lines in April 1958 as a displaced person. He was a shopkeeper, and we lived there with my mother and my siblings—Madan Lal, Puran Kumari, Surinder Kumar, and Baby. Madan Lal was working, and the rest of us were dependents.

My father passed away in 1965. Years later, in March 1972, my mother was given a duplex flat in the same area under a redevelopment scheme. She was supposed to pay Rs. 14,325 in 20 annual instalments with 5% interest, and she also had to give up another quarter she was living in. She never paid the full amount, but she lived in that flat until she passed away in October 1999.

After her death, I found out that my brother Surinder Pal Sharma was saying the flat belongs only to him. He showed a document from 1992, registered at the sub-registrar’s office, saying my mother left everything to him. My husband’s name is on it as a witness. But I never saw this paper when my mother was alive, and I don’t believe she made it. She would never have left out all her children.

I filed a case in 2004 asking that the flat be divided equally among the four of us—me, Surinder Pal, Puran Kumari, and Santosh Rani, who was Madan Lal’s widow. Surinder says the document is real, but no one who was there when it was signed has come forward to say they saw her put her signature. The lawyer who wrote it signed at the bottom, but he didn’t sign as a witness—only as the person who prepared the paper. The other witness, my husband, hasn’t spoken about it either.

I just want my fair share. We were all her children. I have the letter showing she got the flat, and I know how much she paid. I want the flat to be divided properly, because it was never meant to go to just one person.

I own a piece of land in Kolkata, at 243N, Acharya Prafulla Chandra Road. It’s 14 cottahs, 5 chittacks and 40 square feet. My father, Kalidas Sadhu, signed a development agreement in April 1992 with a builder, Sushil Kumar Agarwal. The idea was that he would build a residential complex on our land. We were to keep 42% of the total constructed area, and he would get 58% to cover his costs and profit. He was supposed to get the building plan approved from the Calcutta Municipal Corporation, prepare the design with our approval, and pay us Rs 4 lakh as a deposit — which would be returned once construction was complete.

After the agreement, he found the property had some problems — unpaid municipal taxes, electricity bills, and it had been used as a factory with some worker issues. He told us he would clear these dues and we agreed he could recover the money from his share later. He says he spent over Rs 7 lakh on this, but I don’t have proof of most of it.

Years passed and nothing happened. No construction, no plan approval. In March 2002, my father wrote to him saying he didn’t accept the agreement anymore. Agarwal replied in April 2002, saying it was still valid and asking for authority to move forward. They met and supposedly agreed to change the share — we’d get 47%, he’d get 53%. But there’s no written record of this change.

In May 2003, he sent a notice asking my father to pay part of the plan sanction fees. My father’s lawyer replied in June 2003, saying the agreement was already cancelled on 19 May 2003, and asked Agarwal to return all documents and take back his deposit.

Then, in August 2003, he started legal action. He claimed the cancellation wasn’t valid and wanted to stop us from selling the land to anyone else. Later, he added that he wanted us to go ahead and let him build as per the original deal.

I don’t understand how he can demand this after doing nothing for ten years. He never got the plan approved. He never took possession of the land. We never handed it over. Now he wants to force us to let him build and take more than half the flats. I want to protect my family’s property. I want this matter settled so he can’t block us from using or selling our own land.

I’m a member of the South Delhi Club in Central Park, Greater Kailash-I, New Delhi. The club has been running there for decades. The land and building are not ours — we’ve been using them under a lease from the Lal Chand Public Charitable Trust. The lease started in 1965 for 25 years, and then it was extended through another agreement in 1979. Later, in 1990, a new lease was signed for another 25 years, and it was registered. Under this arrangement, we were supposed to pay a fixed monthly rent every three months, plus 14% of what we collected from members as subscriptions.

Sometime in the mid-1990s, we stopped paying the rent. The Trust sent us letters in late 1996 and early 1997 asking for the money. Then, in July 1997, they sent a formal notice demanding full payment, warning that if we didn’t pay, they would end the lease. We didn’t pay. Another notice came in October 1997, listing all the quarters we had missed — from late 1996 through mid-1997. We still didn’t respond.

In December 1997, they sent a final notice saying the lease was cancelled and we had to vacate. Instead of paying, we decided to challenge their right to collect rent. We filed a case claiming the Trust no longer owned the property and had no authority to lease it to us. We wanted the court to cancel the 1992 lease and stop them from demanding money. But we didn’t follow up properly — we missed hearings and didn’t file our replies on time. That case just stalled.

At the same time, the Trust had filed a case against the club for possession and recovery of unpaid rent. In our response, we admitted we were tenants and had not paid, but said we were ready to deposit the arrears in court. Our lawyer even told the court we would clear the dues. Later, we said we accepted the lease terms and were willing to pay going forward. But we never actually made the payments.

Now, the Trust is insisting we leave the premises. I’ve been using the club for years. So have many other members. We’ve put in time, effort, and money. I don’t think it’s fair to throw us out without giving us a chance to settle the dues and continue. I want to find a way to keep the club where it is and protect our right to stay, especially if we’re ready to pay what’s due.

My name is Meera Bhanja. I am the widow of Dr. Umaprasanna Bhanja. My husband and Dr. Phanindra Nath Choudhury, who was married to Nirmala Kumari Choudhury, were close friends. Back in 1940, they bought two plots of land together in Midnapore—C.S. Plot Nos. 73 and 74. Each plot was meant to be shared equally between them.

Later, on 14 April 1947, Nirmala sold me 5 decimals of Plot No. 74 through a registered document. This wasn’t just a share in the land—it was a specific part, the northern half, and it included a house with three rooms, a kitchen, and a privy. The document clearly says she is selling me that portion out of her half. I have that document with me.

For years, both families used the land, and we even dug a well together. But over time, Nirmala started building structures on the part that belongs to me. She claims the whole plot, even the portion I bought, and won’t let me have peaceful use of it.

I tried to settle this locally, but she refuses to acknowledge my ownership. The land records from the recent survey show that the old C.S. Plot No. 74 has now been split into three new plots. One of them, R.S. Plot No. 1508, is shown as being in my possession. The khatian also lists both our names as joint holders for some of the land, but my 1947 document proves I have a defined portion.

I want to get clear recognition of my ownership over that 5 decimals of land and the house on it. I also want to be able to use and possess that part without interference. I don’t want to be blocked from my own land, especially when I have a registered sale deed and the land records support me. I need help to stop her from building on my portion and to get what rightfully belongs to me.

My name is Murugan. I am one of the sons of Kannan, and I’m speaking for myself and my brothers. Our grandfather, Petha Gounder, owned a piece of land in our village. He had two sons—my father Kannan and our uncle Balaraman—and three daughters. In May 1971, he made a will saying that both Kannan and Balaraman would have the right to live on and use the property during their lives. After both of them passed away, the property was to go to the male children of both sons. If one of them had no male child, then the other’s son would get the full share. Petha Gounder died later that year, in November 1971. His wife, Sengani Ammal, passed away in February 1982.

Balaraman had one son, Palanivel, who was born in July 1978. While Palanivel was still a child, Balaraman sold parts of the property—Items 1 to 3—in December 1981. He also sold Item 6 and part of Item 7 in March 1981 and again in March 1982 to some people we now call the defendants. Balaraman died in 1983, and my father Kannan died in December 1984. Our cousin Palanivel died as a minor, in February 1986. After his death, his mother, Lakshmi Ammal, signed a release deed in March 1986 in our favour, for some money.

We believe that Balaraman had no right to sell the property on behalf of his minor son. A father can’t just sell his child’s share in inherited property like that, especially without any urgent need. Since Palanivel died young and left no children, we believe the property should now come to us as the only surviving male heirs of the other son. The people who bought the land are still in possession, but we say they don’t have full rights over it. We want them to return the property to us. We also want a declaration that we are the rightful owners and that the sales made by Balaraman on behalf of his son are not valid. We want to get back what belongs to us under our grandfather’s will.

My name is Ranvir Dewan, and I need your help with a property matter in our family. The house is at D-246, Defence Colony, New Delhi. It has a basement, ground floor, first floor, and later a third floor was added. My father, B.R. Dewan, built this house and owned it completely in his name.

He had two wives—my mother, Pritam, and his first wife, Kamla Devi. I am the son of Pritam, and I have a sister, Rashmi Khanna, who is also my mother’s daughter. My father had another son, Ashok, from his first marriage.

On 24 June 1984, my father made a Will. In it, he gave me the ground floor of the house and gave the first floor to my sister Rashmi. The Will says we each got full ownership of those parts. For my mother, he said she could live in the house for her entire life, collect rent from it, and use that money to take care of herself and maintain the property. She could also change tenants if needed. But the Will also says she would act as a caretaker for me and my sister, and after she passed away, the house would go back to us as the real owners. It even says we could show our ownership in tax filings.

My father died on 16 September 1984. After that, my mother applied for legal approval of the Will, which was granted a few years later. Following that, my sister and I got our names updated in the municipal records as owners of our respective floors.

Later, we decided to redevelop the house with a builder. A new third floor was built. But after that, my sister started claiming more than her share. She says she owns the first floor outright, which is fine, but she now claims rights over the third floor and the rent from it, and says my mother had no real control over the property.

My mother and I filed a case in 2010 to clarify our rights, especially over the third floor and the income from the property. My mother passed away in 2016. Now, I want to make sure that her rights are protected and that I, as her son, inherit what belongs to her. I have the original Will, the probate papers, and the municipal mutation records. I want the court to confirm that I am entitled to the third floor and its income, and stop my sister from making claims on it.

I bought a plot of land in 1989—1278 square yards in Prehlad Pur Bangar, Delhi. It’s part of Khasra No. 62/19/1. I paid Rs. 40,000 for it and have the sale deed signed by Kaptan Singh, who was acting as attorney for the original owners. Since then, I’ve been in full possession. I built a room and a boundary wall on it long before any government notice came. The land is developed, and it’s within 50 meters of the village abadi of Lal Dora.

In October 1999, the government put out a notice saying they were taking over land in our area, including mine. I objected at the time because there was a government policy from December 1998 that said land like mine—already built up and close to a village—should not be acquired. But they ignored that and issued another notice in April 2000 saying the acquisition was going ahead.

Then in April 2002, the land office passed an order saying the land was being taken. But from that day to now, they have never given me any money for it, and no government official has ever come and taken physical control of the land. I’ve stayed on it, looked after it, and continued using it.

Years later, I heard that the government passed a new rule about land acquisition that says if they don’t pay the owner or take possession within five years of their order, then the takeover no longer stands. My order was in 2002, and it’s now 2014—way more than five years. And since they never paid me or took the land, I believe the acquisition should no longer apply.

I want to be able to keep my land without any threat of being removed. I’ve done nothing wrong—I bought it legally, I’ve been on it for decades, and they never completed what they started. I just want to live in peace and have my rights recognised.

I own a shop in Connaught Place, Delhi. I bought the building in 1958, and since then, a business called Young Friends & Co. has been renting this shop. It was originally taken by someone who’s now deceased, and now it’s being run by Ashu Mohan Gupta and Shashi Gupta. They’ve operated a chemist shop there for years.

Over time, I started noticing that other people were using parts of the shop. Three doctors, including a dentist, began running clinics inside the space. Two other firms were also using it. These weren’t just visitors—they had set up their own practice, with patients coming in regularly. I never agreed to this, and I wasn’t even informed. The rent agreement was only with Young Friends & Co., and they had no right to let others occupy the space, especially not for running separate businesses.

In 1974, I took steps to get my shop back because I believed they had given parts of it to these other people without my permission. I had my managing partner give statements about what was happening. He saw how the doctors were using the space daily, as if they were the ones in charge. But the person handling my case at that time said I hadn’t proven that the tenant had given up control. They said the main tenant was still in charge and that the others were just there with permission and only for a few hours.

Later, another authority reviewed the matter and agreed with me—saying that yes, parts of the shop were being used by others in a way that amounted to sub-letting. But then someone challenged that decision, and now the order in my favour has been set aside.

From 2009 to 2018, they paid me ₹30,000 a month as occupation charges. After that, they stopped. I heard they tried to pay just ₹90, which was the old rent from decades ago, but I didn’t accept it because it didn’t reflect the current situation or the misuse of the property.

I want to get my shop back. I have the purchase documents from 1958 and records showing the rent payments over the years. I just want to regain full control of my property because it’s being used in a way I never allowed.

My name is Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma. I was married to Parayankandiyil Kanhirakunnath Kurungodan Raman Nair. We had five children together. I know he was already married to another woman, Ammu Amma, who had nine children with him. But I was also his wife in every way—our marriage was performed with all the proper customs, we lived together, and people in the community treated us as husband and wife. We lived in a house in Kerala that belonged to him, and I’ve been there with my children all these years.

He passed away on 9th January 1975. After that, his first wife and her children started saying that my marriage wasn’t valid because he was already married when we got married. They claim that since my marriage wasn’t valid, I and our children have no right to any of his property—neither land nor house nor anything else. They went to court and filed cases asking to take over properties that were in his name or that I was living in. They also want a share in the land he held as a tenant.

When they did that, I also went to court to ask for a fair division of his property. I believe I am his wife and my children are his children, so we should get our rightful share. They say that because he was already married, I was just a second wife and not a legal one, and that my children can’t inherit. But we’ve always been part of his family. I have proof of our marriage, people who witnessed it, and records showing we lived together.

All I want is for me and my children to be treated fairly. We’re not asking for more—just what belongs to us. I want to keep living in the house we’ve always lived in, and I want my children to get the share that is rightfully theirs from their father’s property. I don’t want us to be pushed out or treated as if we don’t matter.

I am one of the landowners from Naraina village, and I want to tell you about what happened to our land. In October 1961, the government announced in the official Gazette that they were taking about 3,470 acres in our village for the "planned development of Delhi." A month later, in November 1961, they say they put up notices in the village to inform people about this. Then, years later in December 1966, they made another official announcement saying the land was now fully acquired.

Our family owns 14 bighas in this area. The problem is, we never saw any notice in the village. No one in our community remembers seeing it posted or being told about it publicly. The government says a peon from the land office put up the notice and even had it announced in the village, but the papers they produced don’t match. There are different versions of what was written, and one version doesn’t even mention our village by name. The peon’s own statement from years later doesn’t line up with the official record either.

Also, this land is partly inside the Delhi Cantonment area, which has its own rules for development. The big development plans for Delhi — the one from 1957, the revised one in 1962, and even the later one from 1992 — don’t show our land being used for any specific public project. In fact, the plan says the use of this land is "undetermined." If the government really needed it for public development, why wasn’t it clearly marked in those plans?

All the land around ours was taken and turned into homes — now lakhs of people live there. But our piece was left out, even though it’s in the same area. I feel this was not done fairly. I don’t believe the public notice was properly shared, and I don’t see how they can say this land was truly needed for public use. I want to challenge this because I think we were wrongfully deprived of our property. I want our land back, or at least proper justice if it can’t be returned.

I own a piece of agricultural land in village Nangli Poona, Delhi, measuring 1 bigha and 4 biswas. I’ve been living on it and farming it for years. The land is in my name in the government revenue records, and I’ve paid all dues. My neighbour, Sukhbir Singh, has been trying to take it from me. In April 2005, he went to the police and said I was trespassing on his land, which is not true — it’s my land. They registered a complaint against me, and I was arrested. I got released later, but the case created a lot of trouble for me.

After that, I reported to the police that he had come onto my land and damaged it. They registered my complaint too, and by December 2005, they filed a chargesheet against him. Then, in February 2006, the police closed their inquiry into the case he had started against me, saying there was no evidence. But he didn’t stop. He went to the revenue office in Narela twice — once in June 2006 and again in August 2007 — asking to have his name added in the records as if he were the one using the land. Both times, the officer rejected his request because he has no legal right over it.

I hired a lawyer, Pradeep Rana, to help me deal with the false case. He took some papers from me — I signed them in Hindi because I don’t read or write English well. Later, I found out he filed a second set of papers with the same content as the first, without telling me. When the people handling the matter found out, they called me and my lawyer and asked what happened. I told them I didn’t know about the second filing — I had trusted my lawyer. He admitted he made a mistake and said sorry. They accepted his apology and dropped the issue in February 2009.

Now, six months later, Sukhbir Singh has started another criminal case against me, saying I filed something false. But the same matter was already looked into, and I was cleared. I just want to live in peace on my own land without being dragged into new cases over something that’s already been settled. I want this new case stopped because it’s not fair and it’s only being used to harass me.

I am one of the legal heirs of my mother, Sagunthala, who passed away. We are farmers and have been living in this village in Salem district, Tamil Nadu, for generations. In February, March and May of 1984, the government issued notices saying they were acquiring 196 acres of land, including our family’s land, for expanding a state-owned company called Tamil Nadu Magnesite Limited. At that time, we were told the land was being taken for industrial development.

Our family owns a portion of this land, which has been in our name for many years. It was used for growing crops and was irrigated, so it was good agricultural land. But over time, people started building houses nearby, and two residential colonies came up close to our area. Factories also came up, and the whole region began changing. We believed our land had become suitable for housing, not just farming.

When compensation was decided in 1986, the Land Acquisition Officer valued the land at Rs. 18,000 per acre for irrigated land and Rs. 15,000 for unirrigated land. We felt this was far too low, especially since the land was now near residential and industrial areas. We also noticed that no compensation was given for wells, cement channels, trees, or structures on the land. Some people even had to move out early, but no money was paid for relocation or loss of livelihood.

We asked for a review and submitted sale deeds from nearby areas where land had been sold at much higher rates, showing that the market value was going up. We argued that our land should be treated as potential house sites. A court later agreed and raised the value to Rs. 1,75,000 per acre, considering the location and development around it.

But then a higher court reduced it to Rs. 75,000 per acre, saying the land was still agricultural and that we hadn’t claimed such high amounts earlier. That doesn’t reflect the real value. I want fair compensation that accounts for what the land is actually worth today, considering where it is and how the area has grown. I want the government to pay us what is just.

I am the managing director of Ashoka Marketing Ltd. We’ve been running our business from a portion of a building at 5 Parliament Street, New Delhi since July 1, 1958. The building belonged to Punjab National Bank, and they gave us the space on rent. We’ve been paying rent regularly all these years and have always used it for our office work.

Around 1970, the government took over the bank and made it a government-controlled institution. After that, we continued as tenants, but now the bank was under government control.

In May 1971, the bank sent us a notice saying our tenancy would end on November 30, 1971. After that, they started proceedings to remove us from the premises. We told them that since they are now a government body, their property is treated as public property, and the rules for removing tenants should follow the special law for government or public buildings.

Even though we were already dealing with one set of proceedings, another process was started by the Estate Officer, who handles cases related to public buildings. He passed an order asking us to vacate. We raised our objections through the proper channel, but those were rejected. Later, a higher officer also said we had to leave.

We went to the High Court to explain our side, but they did not help us either. Another company, Sahu Jain Services Ltd., is in the same building and has the same problem. A different person, Mr. K.B. Parsai, was renting space in the Allahabad Bank building at 17 Parliament Street, which is also under government control, and after his three-year term ended in 1982, they started similar action against him. A newspaper company, Bennett Coleman, has been in a building in Darya Ganj since 1948, and even they are now being asked to leave after the insurance company they originally rented from was taken over by the government.

We’ve been there for nearly 30 years, running our business peacefully, paying rent, and not causing any trouble. I don’t understand how we can be treated like unauthorized occupants. I want to stop this eviction and continue working from the same place. I need your help to find out if we have any right to stay and how we can protect ourselves.

I am the owner of a commercial property located in the Great Eastern Hotel building on Hemanta Basu Sarani in Kolkata. It’s a very old heritage building, and my company, Apollo Zipper India Limited, became the owner of the entire property, including this space, in October 2005. This happened because the West Bengal government transferred all the assets of the hotel to my company through an official order. Before that, the government had taken control of the hotel in the 1980s and was managing it through a special authority called GEHA.

One shop in the building, about 6,000 square feet, has been occupied by a company called W. Newman & Co. Ltd. for many decades. They were originally tenants of the old hotel company, but when the government took over in 1980, they started paying rent to the government body, GEHA. They paid Rs. 40,000 every month without any issue until 2005.

After our company took over in 2005, GEHA sent them letters in early 2006 informing them that ownership had changed and that they now had to pay rent to us. They received these letters and never objected. They just stopped paying rent altogether.

In May 2012, I sent them a formal letter asking them to vacate the premises within a month, since they were not paying rent and we needed the space. They did not reply. Even after that, they stayed in the property and didn’t pay anything.

Now, they are saying the rent is only Rs. 1,600 per month, which is not true — they were paying Rs. 40,000 for years. They are also claiming they don’t know who owns the property — us or another company — even though we’ve shown them the government order and letters. They’ve even started a case asking someone to accept this lower rent from them.

I have all the government orders, the transfer documents, and the letters we sent and received. I just want them to leave the property and pay the rent they owe. They’ve had years to raise any issue, but they never did. I don’t see why they should continue living in my property for free.

I am one of the original landowners from a village near Mourigram in West Bengal. Back in 1961, the government acquired 151.18 acres of our land, including my family’s, for a railway project — the Mourigram-Dankuni Link of the South-Eastern Railways. We were compensated at the time, but the land was taken for a specific public purpose. After the railway work was done, the government got back about 77 acres of surplus land from the Railways in 1972. In 1973, most of that surplus — over 74 acres — was handed over to the Animal Husbandry Department, and they planned to set up an abattoir there. That never really took off.

Now, decades later, in 1994, the government leased out 46.42 acres of that same surplus land — land originally taken from us for a railway — to a private company, Enagro Foods (India) Limited, which is linked to a Dubai-based firm called Al-Kabeer. They paid about Rs. 71.6 lakh as lease premium for 99 years, and also bought the Durgapur abattoir’s machinery. But here’s what bothers me: this land is being used for a massive slaughterhouse and food processing plant, which is completely different from the original purpose of the acquisition. There was no public notice, no auction, no open bidding. The deal was done quietly, and we only found out about it years later.

We’ve seen newspaper reports and government letters showing that the company promised to build an integrated food plant, but the main activity is animal slaughter. I believe this violates the understanding under which our land was taken. The government should have either returned the unused surplus to us or sold it publicly. Instead, it’s been handed over to a private party on very soft terms. I feel cheated, and so do many others in the community, especially those of us who are vegetarians and have religious objections to a slaughterhouse on land that once belonged to us. I want the government to stop using this land for slaughter and either return it to the original owners or sell it through a fair, open process.

My father, Samey Singh, owned a house at House No. 163 (Old No. 143), Village Dhakka, Kingsway Camp, Delhi.
