In December 1987, he allowed Brahm Prakash and his family to live in the house for residential use. The monthly rent was Rs. 1,050, not including electricity, water, or house tax. They moved in on 27.12.1987 and paid rent regularly until February 1993. After that, they stopped paying.

In March 1996, my father sent them a written notice asking for the unpaid rent, which had reached Rs. 27,800. The notice was delivered properly, but they did not pay anything. So, in May 1996, my father started a case to evict them for not paying rent. They responded by saying they were not tenants at all — that there was no landlord-tenant relationship.

My father was given several chances to prove he was the owner and that they were living there as tenants paying rent. He was told to bring witnesses to support his claim. But no one came on the scheduled dates, including the last ones in September and November 1997. Because no evidence was presented, the case was closed in January 1998, with a note that the landlord-tenant relationship was not proven. My father did not take any further step after that, and he passed away a few years later.

After his death, I and my family members, as his legal heirs, tried to start a new case in 2001. We claimed rent arrears from March 1993 up to May 2001, based on a fresh notice we had issued. We believed this was a new claim because the unpaid rent had continued to grow. But the tenants objected, saying we cannot bring the same matter again because the earlier case had already decided the issue. They asked for our case to be thrown out.

The officer handling rent cases refused to throw it out, saying the earlier case did not finally decide the issue and that we had a fresh claim. But the tenants went to a higher authority, which ruled against us. That authority said the 1998 decision must be treated as a final finding that my father was not their landlord, and because of that, we cannot try again.

I don’t understand how a case that ended because no one appeared can be treated as a final decision on ownership and tenancy. We have documents showing my father owned the property. The tenants are still living there without paying anything. I want to get them out and recover the money they owe. I need your help to move forward.

I’m Priti Saraf, and I need your help because someone took my money under false promises and now refuses to return it. In December 2011, I entered into an agreement with Sunita Goyal to buy part of her property at 37, Friends Colony (East), New Delhi. The land is large—3930 square yards—but she wanted to sell me 1205.43 square yards for Rs. 63.28 crores. She told me the property was mortgaged to State Bank of Patiala for about Rs. 18 crores and that she needed my payment to clear the loan and get the land free.

We signed the agreement on 24th December 2011. I paid her Rs. 12.5 crores right away by cheque. The agreement said she had to complete three things by 24th March 2012—get the bank’s clearance, submit plans for dividing the plot, and get official approval. Only after that would I pay more. But she missed the deadline. Even so, I paid her another Rs. 5.4 crores in May 2012 because she kept assuring me everything was being done. As a guarantee, she gave me post-dated cheques worth Rs. 25.5 crores.

Later, I found out she used my money to clear her bank loan and got the NOC, but never told me. Worse, she never actually applied to divide the land—because it’s not allowed under city rules. The plot can’t be split without official permission, and she never got it. Instead of moving forward, she suddenly cancelled the deal in January 2013 and refused to return my money.

I tried to settle it, but she ignored me. So I filed a complaint, and after some time, the police registered a case based on my complaint. They investigated and confirmed she had taken money from another buyer the same way in 2007 and backed out. The police filed a chargesheet saying this was fraud.

But now, the matter has been stopped on the grounds that it’s just a business dispute. I don’t think this is fair—she took my money with no real plan to sell me the land. I want the case to go forward so I can prove this was not just a broken deal, but a deliberate cheat. I want her to be held accountable and to get my money back.

I am Daljit Singh, and I want to sell a piece of land I own in Mohan Cooperative Industrial Estate on Mathura Road in New Delhi. The property is A-22, and it’s about 19,075 square yards. I used to run a business there called South Delhi Toyota, which was a franchise for selling Toyota cars. The business and the land together were valuable.  

In April 2005, the people from Hari Steel and General Industries Ltd, especially their Managing Director, approached me saying they wanted to buy the entire setup — the land, the building, and the business with the franchise rights. We agreed on a total price of ₹55.50 crores. On April 7, 2005, I received ₹2 crores from them — ₹1 crore by cheque and ₹1 crore in cash. Their Managing Director acknowledged this payment.  

Then, on May 3, 2005, we signed a formal written agreement to sell. In that document, it clearly says they had already paid ₹5 crores in total. That includes the ₹2 crores paid earlier and an additional ₹3 crores paid on the day of signing, which I received in cash. The agreement breaks down the amount: ₹49 crores for the land and building, ₹6.50 crores for the business and franchise, and the rest for the difference in assets and liabilities, which we agreed to settle later based on the balance sheet.  

After that, I was ready to complete the sale. I kept asking them to pay the remaining amount and close the deal, but they kept delaying. Instead of paying, they started saying the agreement was fake, that some of the signatures were forged, and that they never agreed to the full terms. They even claimed they never received ₹3 crores in cash, which is not true.  

Later, another person, Praveen Kumar Jolly, came forward saying he had an earlier agreement for part of the land, but that doesn’t cancel my deal. I’ve always been willing and ready to sell as per the 2005 agreement. I just want them to pay the remaining ₹50.50 crores and take the sale deed. That’s all I’m asking for.

I own a piece of land in South Madras, about half an acre, which has been in my family for generations. My grandfather bought it in the 1930s, and we’ve used it for farming and rented out a small portion for housing. In early 1975, I started seeing government officials walking around, measuring the land, and putting up notices. Over that year, three different notices were issued saying the government was taking our land for housing projects — one called the "Kalaignar Karunanidhi Nagar Further Extension Scheme," another for a new part of that colony, and a third for improving housing in South Madras. But none of these notices showed any actual plan — no map, no layout, no details about what would be built or how much land they wanted.

A few years later, some officers came and held a meeting where people could speak up about the land. I went and told them I didn’t agree because I didn’t know what these housing plans really were. At that time, there was no approved project or published design from the housing board. I only found out later that the plans were made *after* the government started taking the land, not before.

Years passed. Nothing happened for a long time. Then, in 1983, they finally told us how much money we’d get as compensation. The amount is very low — nowhere near what the land is worth today. I feel this whole process was unfair. They claimed it was for public housing, but how can that be proper if there was no real plan when they started? The people whose land is being taken should know exactly why and for what purpose, so they can respond properly.

I have the original sale documents from my grandfather, the revenue records showing our name, copies of the notices they put out, and the letter stating the compensation. I want to stop this takeover or, if that’s not possible, get proper compensation and a fair process. I don’t think what they did was right, and I want someone to help me get justice.

I am the tenant of a commercial building at door numbers 16 and 17 on Poonamallee High Road in Madras. My business, Raval & Co, has been running from this place since May 1929. At that time, the owner was someone else, not the people who own it now. We didn’t have a registered document back then, but in 1935, we signed a proper lease that was registered. That lease says it will last until May 1, 1969, and after that, we have the right to renew it for another 15 years on the same terms.

The rent was fixed at Rs. 225 per month. We also agreed to pay Rs. 225 every year for repairs and Rs. 220 for taxes and other local charges. In 1949, both sides agreed that we would pay 25% more in rent, plus some other small amounts. This was not written into the lease, but we’ve been paying it regularly, and they’ve been accepting it without any issue.

The current owners bought the property in 1962. Not long after that, they started a process to get a “fair rent” decided by an official authority. They say they have the right to do this even though we already have a lease with clear terms and it hasn’t ended yet.

I don’t see how they can go to this authority to change the rent we’ve already agreed upon. We’ve always paid on time and followed the terms of our lease. The lease is still running, and we want to continue under it. I just want to be left alone to run my business as we have for over 40 years. I don’t want any interference or attempts to change the rent we’ve been paying under our agreement. I want to protect the rights we have under that lease and stop them from trying to get a new rent fixed through this process.

I own a piece of land in Madrampura, Jaipur — 14 bighas and 16 biswas, Khasra No. 383. My company, Swaika Properties Pvt. Ltd., holds this land. In June 1975, the government sent a notice saying they wanted to take our land for extending the Civil Lines area and building a housing scheme. They sent another notice in August 1975 with the same purpose. We responded right away in September 1975, saying we objected, and we kept sending letters over the years asking them to stop the process, but they never gave us a proper reply.

In February 1984, they issued another notice saying the acquisition was confirmed. After that, they told us to hand over the land. We refused because we never agreed to sell it. We tried to raise our issue with a court in Calcutta, but they said they couldn’t deal with land matters in Rajasthan, so that didn’t work out.

They claim they took possession of the land on 17th February 1987 and gave it to the Jaipur Development Authority. But that’s not true — we were still on the land, managing it, and no one legally took control from us. In 1987, we started another process in Rajasthan to challenge what they were doing, but we paused it for a short time so we could refile properly. Within four months, in July 1989, we started the process again.

Then, in mid-1989, they passed an award saying how much compensation they would pay, and they say the government approved it in July 1989. But we were never part of that process, and we never accepted any money. We’ve been fighting this since 1975 — we’ve objected every step of the way. We have our ownership papers, sale records, and copies of all the letters we sent.

I want to stop this takeover and get my land back because the whole process was done without following the proper steps, and we were never given a fair chance to speak or be compensated.

My name is Ganesan, and I need your help regarding a piece of land in Coimbatore. The property is part of a larger plot that was originally bought in 1922 in the name of a man called Byrammal. Over time, it became a family holding, but I believe a portion of it—specifically the eastern half—came into the personal ownership of Masaney Gowder, who was the father of two sisters, Amasaveni and Attiammal.

On 29 January 1969, Masaney Gowder made a will giving his share of the property to those two sisters. I have a copy of that will, and I know it was properly signed. Two people signed at the bottom as witnesses when it was made. After he passed away, the sisters inherited that half of the land based on the will. They were in possession and treated it as their own.

In 1981, my wife Kamalam and I bought that half from them. We have a registered sale deed, and we paid them a fair price. Right after the sale, we took possession. We’ve been using our portion ever since—keeping it clean, storing our things, and making sure it’s maintained. We’ve also been paying the property taxes.

But Ayyasamy and his brother Shanmugam, who are related to the same family, are now saying the will is not valid. They claim the land was always joint family property and that Masaney Gowder had no right to leave it to his daughters by will. They also say the sisters never actually used the land, which isn’t true. And they’re now trying to stop us from staying on the portion we bought.

I just want to be able to keep using the half we purchased without being harassed or thrown out. I want the will to be accepted as genuine, and I want our ownership to be recognized. We have the documents and we’ve acted in good faith. I need this resolved so we can live in peace on the land we rightfully own.

My family’s business, M.V.R. Group of Industries, took a loan from Indian Bank in 1992. As part of that, the bank says we gave our property as security by handing over the title papers in 1995 or 1996. When the business couldn’t repay, the bank started recovery steps in 1996. Later, in December 2004, they sent a notice demanding payment, and in March 2005, another notice saying they were taking control of the property.

In August 2006, two of my relatives gave a registered Power of Attorney to a man named S.P. Velayutham. That document clearly said he was not allowed to sell the property or create any charge on it. But in July 2007, he sold the property to his son Amar anyway, using that same Power of Attorney. The sale deed was registered at the sub-registrar’s office, even though he had no authority to sell. Then, in October 2008, Amar made a settlement deed and transferred the property back to his father.

Around the same time, Indian Bank had assigned all its rights over the loan and the property to a company called Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited in 2007. Now this company says they have the right to take over our property. They issued their own sale notice in August 2008. But instead of going to a civil court where property disputes are normally settled, they went to a higher court and got an order saying the 2007 sale registration should be cancelled. They claimed the sub-registrar should have checked the Power of Attorney and seen that the sale wasn’t allowed.

But there are already civil cases filed by our family members challenging these transactions, and that company joined those cases. There have also been local disputes over who is in possession, and police-related proceedings happened because of people entering the land. What’s more, a court in a CBI case convicted some bank officials and borrowers in 1998 for fraud, forgery, and corruption, which raises serious questions about whether the original mortgage was even real.

I don’t see how this company can skip the normal process and go to a higher court when the issue is about ownership and sale — something that should be decided in a civil case. They’re not saying the government did something wrong — they’re fighting over who owns the land. I want them to be stopped from taking this shortcut and be made to resolve this where it belongs — in a civil court, through a proper trial.

I rented a flat on the first floor of a house at C-62, Maharani Bagh, New Delhi, along with a garage and a servant’s quarter above it. I’ve been paying Rs.1,000 per month since 1974—Rs.950 as rent and Rs.50 for the booster pump. The owner, Smt. Khatoon Quamarain, filed a case in January 1977 to evict me, saying she needed the flat for herself because she had no other suitable place to live. She claimed she was living with her niece in Nizammuddin East, in a small two-bedroom house with a shared bathroom, and that her niece wanted her mother to move in, so she couldn’t stay there permanently. She also said she was a social worker and needed space for her work.

But I don’t believe her. She’s not poor—she comes from a well-off family, has bank savings, and her son is a senior government officer living in Delhi since 1976. He stays at the External Affairs Hostel, but she could easily live with him. Instead, she’s trying to get me out just so she can charge higher rent. The ground floor of the same building was rented out to the New Zealand Embassy for Rs.2,500 a month, and after they left in 1977, she kept re-renting it to others—first to Shri Dalmia, then to Indian Express, and later to Shri Ganeriwal—at even higher rates. If she really needed a home, why didn’t she move into the ground floor when it was vacant? Why keep it rented out for income?

Earlier, in 1974, she tried to evict a company I was associated with, claiming the same need, but that case failed. Now she’s back with the same story. I think this is all about money. She even tried to force me to pay Rs.2,500 instead of Rs.1,500 at one point. I have documents showing her past claims and rental agreements. I’ve lived here peacefully and paid rent on time. I want to continue living here. I don’t think her claim of personal need is honest. I need your help to fight this so I’m not thrown out unfairly.

My name is Pratap Singh. I’m the eldest son of the late Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha. After my father was removed from power in 1928, I became the ruler of the state. I want to settle the ownership of two properties—one in Shimla called ‘Sterling Castle’ and another in Delhi at House No. 34, Alipur Road. I believe these belong to me as part of my inheritance, but my mother and brothers are now claiming a share, and I need this resolved.

The Shimla property was bought in 1921. At that time, my father couldn’t buy land outside Nabha in his own name because of British rules, so he arranged for it to be purchased in the name of his friend, Dr. Tehl Singh. The money came from my father, and everyone in the family knew this. In 1952, Dr. Tehl Singh signed a document giving up his name on the property and confirming that it belonged to my father’s family. After my father passed away in 1942, I treated this property as part of my rightful holding. In 1962, I sold it to a charitable organization for Rs 50,000. They later sold it to other people.

The Delhi house was bought in 1922, again not in my father’s name but in the name of a man called Gurnarain Singh Gill. The full amount—Rs 1,25,000—was paid by my father. The property was always looked after by officials from Nabha State. Even after I became ruler, it was managed as part of the estate. When the princely states merged with India in 1948, I included both properties in the list of my private holdings, as was expected.

My mother, Sarojini Devi, and my brothers say these were my father’s personal properties and that they are entitled to a share. But in our family, the eldest son inherits the chiefship and the associated properties. I’ve been in possession of these properties for many years. I want to be declared the rightful owner and stop them from making claims. I also want to recover the benefits they’ve taken from the properties during this dispute.

I am the owner of a property in Park Street, Kolkata, which I got through a company called Park Street Properties Pvt Ltd. The property was originally owned by another company, Karnani Properties Limited, who leased it to my company, and we had the right to sublet it. In October 2004, we entered into an agreement with two brothers, Dipak Kumar Singh and his brother, to let them use the premises for their Blue Fox Restaurant. That agreement was later cancelled because they wanted to run a McDonald’s franchise instead.  

So, on 7th August 2006, we signed a new agreement letting them use the same premises for the McDonald’s business. The rent was Rs. 20,000 per month, payable by the 7th of every month. The agreement said that if they failed to pay rent for three consecutive months or broke any other term, I could give them a 30-day notice to fix the problem, and if they didn’t, I could end the tenancy.  

They have been in possession since August 2006, but they stopped paying rent regularly. In October 2008, after repeated defaults, I gave them a notice under the law, asking them to vacate within 15 days. They didn’t leave. I then filed a case to get back possession of the property and claim the unpaid rent.  

They are now saying that even though the agreement wasn’t registered, it had a clause that the rent would go up by 15% every three years, which they claim shows it was meant to be a long-term lease—maybe even 30 years. They also say I encouraged them to spend a lot of money renovating the place for the McDonald’s outlet, so I shouldn’t be allowed to throw them out now.  

But the truth is, we never agreed to a fixed term of 30 years. The agreement was month-to-month, and they were always supposed to pay on time. They’ve been violating the terms, and I followed the proper process to end the tenancy. I just want to get my property back and stop this continued occupation without proper payment. I need your help to enforce my rights as the landlord.

I’m Aftab Singh, and I want to tell you about a property I paid for but never got. In 2008, I applied to buy a villa from a builder called Emaar MGF in Sector 106, Mohali. On May 6, 2008, we signed an agreement for the sale. I paid all the money they asked for, as per the terms. They promised to hand over the villa by 2011, but till today, I haven’t received possession. The house isn’t ready, and there’s no clear date for when it will be.

In an earlier letter they sent me, dated February 2, 2008, they said that once the final cost was worked out, any extra money I paid would be adjusted. That amount comes to Rs. 2,63,165. They also agreed to pay a penalty of Rs. 1,500 per month for every month they were late in giving me the villa after 2011. It’s now been 55 months of delay, so that’s Rs. 83,500 more. I want them to adjust both these amounts, settle the final account, and return whatever balance is left — with 18% interest from February 6, 2010, which is two years after our agreement.

In July 2015, I filed a complaint with the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission asking for these things. They issued a notice to the builder in November 2015. When they appeared, instead of answering my complaint, the builder asked that the case be sent to private arbitration, saying we had agreed to that in the sale document. But I never agreed to give up my right to come to a consumer forum. I’m not a business — I’m a homebuyer who paid hard-earned money for a home that was promised but not delivered.

I want the builder to give me possession of the villa, adjust the excess payment and the delay penalty, refund the balance with interest, and pay me Rs. 20 lakh for the mental stress and trouble I’ve been through. I also want them to pay the cost of filing this complaint. I just want what was promised to me.

I own a commercial property in Noida—Plot No. 154-B, Block A, Sector 63, Phase III. It was originally leased by NOIDA in 2003, and I got the lease transferred into my name in April 2011. Since then, I’ve held long-term lease rights over the land and the building on it. I live in Kenya and have been managing the property from abroad.

In November 2018, I signed a sub-lease agreement with a company called Hipad Technology India Private Limited. They took over the property for their business, and we agreed on terms like rent, duration, and maintenance. The agreement also included a process for resolving disputes—if we couldn’t settle things through discussion within 21 days, the matter would go to arbitration in Delhi, conducted in English, and decided by one arbitrator we both agree on. If we couldn’t agree on who that person should be, the agreement says someone will be appointed to do it.

By the end of 2019, the company started falling behind on payments and wasn’t following other parts of the agreement. I sent them a formal notice on 11 December 2019, listing their defaults and asking to start arbitration as we had agreed. I even suggested a retired judge, Justice Mukul Mudgal, as the arbitrator, and invited them to respond. But they haven’t replied at all—no objection, no counter-suggestion, nothing.

The issue is about their failure to meet the terms we both signed, not about eviction or any government tenancy protection. The property isn’t covered by any special rent or tenancy law. I just want the arbitration to begin so we can resolve this fairly. Since they’re not responding, I need help getting someone appointed to oversee the arbitration. That’s why I’m reaching out to you.

I’m Shanmugavelu, and I run a company called Sunbright Designers Private Limited. In late 2016, I decided to buy a piece of industrial land in Chennai from a bank auction. The property is in Thiru Vi Ka Industrial Estate, Alandur, about 10,581 square feet, with some sheds on it. It was being sold by Central Bank of India because the previous owner had taken a loan and failed to repay it.

The auction was held online on 7th December 2016. I placed a bid of Rs. 12.27 crores, which was the highest. On the same day, the bank confirmed me as the successful buyer. I paid Rs. 3.06 crores right away as earnest money through RTGS, as required. Their letter said I had to pay another Rs. 2.10 crores within 24 hours—which I did—and the remaining Rs. 9.20 crores within 15 days. It also said clearly that if I didn’t pay the full amount, the sale would be cancelled and the money I’d already paid would be taken by the bank.

I ran into difficulty arranging the rest of the money because the loan I was depending on from another bank was still being processed. So, I emailed the bank on 19th December 2016, asking for three more months to pay. They agreed and wrote back on 20th December, saying I could pay by 7th March 2017 instead. But they also said no further extensions would be allowed, and if I didn’t pay by then, the sale would be cancelled and the money would not be returned.

I couldn’t arrange the full amount by that date. The bank cancelled the sale and kept the entire Rs. 3.06 crores I had paid. I’ve asked them several times to return at least part of it, since I did make a serious attempt and even got their approval for more time. But they’ve refused, saying the terms allowed them to keep everything.

I feel this is unfair. I want to know if there’s any way to get back some of the money or challenge the bank’s decision to take it all.

My name is Ramasamy, and I need your help with a piece of land that I believe I have a right to. The property is in our village, and it’s been with our family since 1956. That’s when my father, Sengoda Gounder, got it through a settlement from his wife’s uncle, Kumarasamy Gounder. There’s a written document for that—dated 7 April 1956—which we have. From the time my father got it, we all treated the land as something the whole family shared. I lived on it, worked on it, and so did my younger brother, Subramanian. My father never kept it separate—he never said it was only his.

We all lived together as one household. At one point, we even took a loan together using the land, and I have records showing that. I always believed that this property belonged to the three of us—me, my father, and my brother—as part of our family holdings. But after my father passed away, my brother started saying that the land was only my father’s personal property and that he, Subramanian, owns it all.

He’s shown two documents—settlement deeds he says my father made in his favour—and a will dated 8 November 2004, also in his name. But I never saw these documents when my father was alive, and I don’t believe he had the right to give away the entire land like that, especially if it had already become part of our shared family property.

When I found out he was planning to sell the land or transfer it, I got worried. I didn’t want him taking away my share, so I went to the local court first to stop him from doing anything with the property. Then I filed another case asking for the land to be divided properly between me and my brother, with each of us getting a fair share.

I have documents that refer to the land as “Pidhirajyam,” which means ancestral property. I also have records of the loan, tax payments, and other papers showing we all used the land together. My brother says we were never a joint family, but that’s not true—we lived and worked on this land as one family for decades.

I just want my rightful share. I don’t want him keeping everything based on documents made secretly. I want the land divided fairly between me and him.

I am the managing director of Thomson Press (India) Ltd. In early 2001, we bought about 4,000 square feet on the first floor of a building in Connaught Place, New Delhi—F-26, known as Sawhney Mansion—from Mrs. Lakhbir Sawhney and her son H.S. Sawhney. We paid for it by clearing their bank loan of around Rs. 1.48 crores with Vijaya Bank, and also settled their income tax dues. Five sale deeds were signed between January 31 and April 3, 2001, transferring the property to us.

Before we bought it, our group company, Living Media India Limited (LMI), had been trying to lease the same space since 1988. At that time, the place was occupied by Peerless General Finance Company, which had a lease and a security deposit of about Rs. 25 lakhs. The Sawhneys promised LMI they would give possession once Peerless left. When they later refused to go ahead with the lease, LMI took them to court. A court order came in April 1991 allowing LMI to take over the property on lease, and they’ve been in possession since then.

Now, someone called Nanak Builders claims they had signed an agreement with the Sawhneys back in May 1986 to buy the same area for Rs. 50 lakhs. They say they paid Rs. 1 lakh and that the rest was to be paid later. They also say they put a notice in *The Hindustan Times* in February 1990 about their deal. We found out about that notice because LMI sent the Sawhneys a legal notice in June 1990, referring to it, and demanding they honour the lease.

Even though the Sawhneys were dealing with this claim, they sold the property to us ten years later. We had no idea there was any active legal case when we completed the purchase. After learning about Nanak Builders’ claim, we tried to get involved in the matter so we could present our side. But we were told we can’t take part. That doesn’t seem fair. We’ve paid a large sum and now risk losing everything. I want to know what we can do to protect our rights as buyers who acted in good faith.

I own a piece of land in Mogappair Village, Sedapet Taluk, in Survey Nos. 340, 341 and 343. My family has held this land for many years. In 1975, the government put out a notice saying they were taking over a large area, including my land, for a housing project called the Ambattur Neighborhood Scheme. I didn’t object at the time. In 1978, they confirmed the acquisition and paid me compensation for my land.

Years went by—almost two decades—and I saw that no houses or buildings were ever constructed on my land. It just remained empty. I heard that one of the other landowners had gone to a higher court and won, because the government had missed a deadline in the process. I wasn’t part of that, but I thought I should try to get my land back since nothing was being done with it.

Around 1997, I asked the government to confirm that my land was no longer needed for the project. I was told I could apply to have it returned, as long as I repaid the compensation they had paid me, plus interest. In February 1999, I sent a formal request to the Housing and Urban Development Department in Chennai, asking them to give the land back to me.

They passed my request to the Tamil Nadu Housing Board. The Board replied that they still planned to use the land for housing—some for low-income families and some for multi-storey flats. Based on that, the government wrote to me in March 1999 saying my request was rejected.

I couldn’t accept that. After so many years of inaction, how can they say the land is still needed? I’ve seen that some other people who owned land in the same area have already gotten their plots back. That doesn’t seem fair. The land was taken for a specific purpose, and that purpose hasn’t been fulfilled.

I want my land returned. I’m ready to pay back the money they gave me, with 9% interest, just like others have done. I’ve waited long enough. The land has been sitting unused for decades, and I believe it should come back to me.

I own a piece of agricultural land in village Chhalera Banger in Ghaziabad district, Uttar Pradesh. It’s about 1.5 acres, and my family has been farming it for generations. We have a patta in my name, and I’ve been paying land revenue regularly. This land has always been ours, and there’s no dispute over that.  

Back in 1987, the government put out a notice saying they needed land in our village for planned industrial development through NOIDA. At that time, people were given a chance to raise objections — we all came forward, submitted our papers, and the process went on for a couple of years. Then, in 1989, they issued another notice confirming the acquisition of those lands, after holding hearings and looking into the objections.  

But just days after that, NOIDA wrote to the government saying they now urgently needed 494 more acres from our village, including my plot, for developing Sector 43 and other parts of the project. Then, in 1990, they issued a new notice saying my land was being taken. This time, they didn’t allow any objections. No one was given a chance to speak, no inquiry was held, and they said it was because of “urgency.”  

But there’s nothing urgent about this. This is part of a long-term plan — they’ve been acquiring land in phases since the 1970s. If it was so urgent, why did they follow the full process just a year earlier?  

Also, my land is not empty or unused. There’s a small house on it — it’s part of the village habitation, with water, electricity, and a boundary wall. I’ve lived there with my family. I’ve heard that the government had a policy not to acquire such village land, especially from families like ours who’ve lived there for years.  

I don’t want my land taken without a fair process. I want to be heard. I want the authorities to follow the proper steps and not just push us out without giving us a chance to present our case. I want to stop this acquisition unless they do it the right way.

I’ve been running a pharmacy from a shop in Coimbatore since 1998. We’ve rented it all these years and always paid rent on time. The owner, N. Magudeswari, never had any problem with us staying there. In February 2012, we signed a new lease agreement to continue the tenancy, and she signed it too—we have a copy of that document.

But in November 2013, she sent us a notice saying the 2012 lease was forged and demanding we leave the shop. We replied in January 2014, explaining that the lease was genuine and we were legitimate tenants. Right after that, she went to the police and filed a complaint saying I forged her signature and threatened her. That same day, she and her husband came to the shop with some men trying to force us out—we stood our ground and didn’t let them.

A few days later, the police called me and the others to the station. They pressured us and made us sign a paper on January 29, 2014, saying we’d settle the matter. We were scared and didn’t feel we had a choice. Then in March 2014, they called us again to the same office, still under pressure, and made us agree to leave the shop by October 31, 2015, as long as we kept paying rent until then. That agreement was written down and signed.

She later sent a letter in October 2015 reminding us to vacate by the deadline. But we believe that entire agreement was forced—we only signed because of the police pressure. We want to keep running our business from this shop. We have our rent receipts, the 2012 lease, and a copy of her police complaint. We just want to be able to stay and prove that we are rightful tenants. I need help to stop them from using that agreement to throw us out.

I am the owner of Bharat Sales Ltd., a business I’ve run from a shop in Delhi for many years. We started using the premises in the 1950s. The building belongs to the Life Insurance Corporation of India, and they’ve always been our landlord. We’ve paid rent regularly and used the space only for our business.  

In the mid-1960s, they started saying we had given part of the shop to someone else to use independently. That’s not true. We never handed over any portion of the space to another person or business. We’ve always been in full control. Some of our employees and family members have used small parts of the area for storage or work, but they were always under our supervision. No one else ever ran their own operation from there.  

We never took any money from anyone for using the space. There was no written agreement with anyone else, no rent received, nothing like that. We continued to manage everything — repairs, electricity, daily use. The place was always ours in practice, and we treated it as our own business location.  

Despite all this, the landlord began proceedings to remove us, claiming we had let someone else take over part of the shop. But they can’t show any proof that we transferred possession or got any payment. No documents, no receipts, no independent person running a separate business from the premises.  

This has gone on for years, and now they’re trying to take the shop away from us based on these old claims. But we’ve done nothing wrong. We’ve always used the place ourselves and followed all the terms we agreed to.  

I want to keep running my business from this shop. I want to be left in peace to continue using the property like we always have. I don’t want to be forced out of a place we’ve occupied and maintained for decades, just because of false allegations.

I am Provash Chandra Dalui, and I have been using a small piece of land at 512/A Russa Road, now known as 34/A Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Road, in Calcutta, since 1946. The land is 6 cottas 5 chittaks and 30 square feet. I took it on lease from Narendra Nath Mukherjee under a registered lease deed dated 26th September 1946. The lease started on 1st April 1946 for 10 years at Rs.200 per month. The deed said that if I paid rent regularly and followed all the rules, the lease would extend for another 5 years, and then another 5 years—so up to 31st March 1966. Each extension had higher rent: Rs.250 for the second term, Rs.300 for the third, and if I wanted to stay one more year after that, it would be at Rs.500.

But I never paid any rent above Rs.200. I always paid on time, but only that amount. I never signed anything for higher rent or agreed to it. In 1959, the original landlord sold the land to Biswanath Banerjee, who became the new owner. I kept paying Rs.200 every month and continued using the land. I built a structure on it for my business.

Now, the new owner is trying to remove me, saying I didn’t exercise the option to extend for one more year at Rs.500. But that doesn’t apply to me. From 1949, when the new tenancy rules came in, I became a protected tenant. The original landlord admitted this in two earlier cases before the tenancy authority—once in 1953 and again in 1958—where he called me a thika tenant. Later, when he tried to claim the higher rent in a case, the court rejected it. I have the lease deed and all the records of my payments. I’ve been here for decades, running my business. I want to continue using the land. I shouldn’t be thrown out after all this time when the owner himself once accepted my status.

I am Nazir Mohamed, and I want to tell you about a piece of land and building at Door No.4, R.S. No.120/13, Mela Senia Street, Aduthurai in Tamil Nadu. My father, M. Abdul Aziz, bought this property in February 1938 through a registered sale deed. From that time, we have lived on the property as owners, not as tenants. The local tax records have always shown my father’s name as the person responsible for the property. After he passed away, I took over everything. In March 1966, I got a registered release deed that formally transferred the property to me from my father’s side of the family. Since then, I’ve been managing it, paying taxes, and living there without any dispute — until recently.

In 1994, J. Kamala, who claims to be the daughter of someone I don’t know well, started making claims about the property. She says her father bought half of it in September 1940 from a man named Rajagopala Pattar, who supposedly got it through a court auction. She says my father was only renting the place from her father and that I’ve been living there without paying rent. She demanded Rs.900 for past use of the property and wants to take control of half of it.

But there was never any agreement between our families about rent. We’ve never paid her or her family anything. No receipts, no contracts, no demands — nothing. The tax payments have always been in our name, not hers. She hasn’t shown any proof that she or her father ever paid taxes on the property either.

Now she’s insisting she owns half and wants money from me for using it. I don’t understand how she can claim ownership when I have the 1938 sale deed, the 1966 release deed, and decades of tax records in my family’s name. I’ve been on this property my whole life, and so was my father before me. I want to make sure no one can take any part of this property or force me to pay her anything. I want to be recognized as the full owner, free from her claims.

I am a landowner in Tamil Nadu, and my family has been farming our land for generations. It’s a small piece of agricultural land in a rural area, and it’s our only source of income. A few years ago, I started getting notices from the government saying they wanted to acquire the land for public purposes—first for an industrial project, and later for road development. They cited old state laws from 1997 and 2001, which allow the government to take land under certain conditions.

At the time, I didn’t understand why they weren’t following the newer rules that came in around 2013, which promised better compensation and support for people who lose their land. That central law was supposed to apply to all land acquisitions, but the state government passed its own amendment in 2014 saying that the old state laws would still apply here. That change was approved by the President and applied from 2014 onwards.

Then, in 2019, after some legal developments I didn’t fully understand, the state passed another law trying to bring back those old 1997 and 2001 laws and make them work again, even for cases that had already been stopped. This new law was made to apply from 2013—before it was even passed—and said all past actions under those old laws should be treated as valid.

What I find troubling is that the government is now acting as if those old laws were never set aside. They’re moving forward with taking land based on laws that, as far as I know, were no longer in force. The new 2019 law doesn’t include key protections like assessing the social impact, setting time limits for the process, or ensuring fair treatment for affected families. People in other parts of the country get these benefits, but we’re being treated differently.

I don’t think the government should be able to revive old laws just by passing a new one that pretends they were always valid. That seems like it goes against how the system should work. I want someone to stop this process and confirm that my land can’t be taken under laws that no longer apply. I want fairness—the same fairness the 2013 law promised to everyone else.

We are the legal heirs of Kewal Chand Mimani, and I want to tell you about a piece of land in Howrah, West Bengal. My grandfather took this land on a 50-year lease from the Dawan family back in 1939. It’s about 8 bighas, and we’ve been using it ever since to run a weekly market called Mangla Hat, which happens every Tuesday. The market was our family’s livelihood.

In November 1987, a fire completely destroyed the market. Just after that, in late November, the local government stepped in and took control of the land, saying they needed it under some old law. We didn’t agree with this takeover, so we started taking steps to challenge it through the legal system. We got our lawyers to file something to stop the government from keeping the land, but it didn’t work. So we kept pushing, and our case was being looked at by the higher court in Calcutta for many years.

During all this time, the government held the land, and we couldn’t use it. Our lease from 1939 was supposed to last until 2009, but even after 1989, we considered ourselves the rightful people in charge because we were the ones who had been running the market and maintaining the place.

Then, in May 1997, we were told that the higher court in Calcutta had said the government’s takeover was not valid because the law they used no longer existed. The court said the land should be given back to the owner or the person who was using it — the occupier. We believe that includes us.

But now the Dawan family, the owners, are saying the land should go only to them. Their lawyer sent a letter claiming full rights. The government officer in charge says he doesn’t know who to give the land to because both sides are claiming it, so he’s not doing anything for now.

We also have a written agreement with the Dawans to buy this land, and we want to go through with that. But first, we need to make sure our right to be in possession is protected. I want your help to get the land back or to make sure we’re not pushed out after all these years.

My name is Satya Pal Anand. I want to tell you about a piece of land that was allotted to my mother, Smt. Veeravali Anand, way back in 1962. It’s Plot No. 7-B in Punjabi Bagh, Raisen Road, Bhopal, given to her by the Punjabi Housing Cooperative Society Ltd. through a registered deed on 22nd March 1962. My mother lived there and treated it as her own property. She passed away on 12th June 1988, and as her legal heir, I inherited this plot.

Years later, in August 2001, the Society suddenly executed a Deed of Extinguishment on 9th August 2001, cancelling my mother’s allotment. They did this unilaterally, saying she violated their rules because no construction was done on the plot within a certain time. But I was never informed or consulted. Then, in April 2004, they allotted the same plot to Mrs. Manjit Kaur and got that deed registered. I objected immediately. Eventually, we reached a compromise in July 2004, and I received Rs. 6.50 lakh — Rs. 4.50 lakh by demand draft and Rs. 2 lakh by post-dated cheque. But that was only to settle interim issues; I never gave up my claim to ownership.

Even after that, I filed a dispute under the Madhya Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act in 2005, before the Deputy Registrar, claiming that the Society had no right to cancel my mother’s allotment and that I am the rightful owner. That case is still pending. During this time, in July 2006, the Society went ahead and transferred the plot again — this time to Mr. S.C. Sharma and Mrs. Meenakshi — and got that deed registered too.

In February 2008, I asked the Sub-Registrar to cancel the registration of the 2001 Extinguishment Deed and the later deeds from 2004 and 2006, since they were based on an invalid cancellation. But he refused, saying he had no power to cancel registered documents, especially since a dispute was already pending. I appealed to the Inspector General of Registration, who also rejected my application, saying his role was only supervisory.

I want to clear my name and establish that I am the rightful owner of this plot. The Society had no right to cancel my mother’s allotment after her death, especially without notice to me. I want those registered deeds cancelled and my ownership recognised.

I am a businessman running a company called M/S Amrit Lal & Co. We have been using a commercial property in Delhi for our business since many years. We rent it from a company called M/S Ambalal Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. The monthly rent we pay is Rs. 8,625. We have always paid the rent on time and have not done anything wrong as a tenant.

Back in 1985, the landlord started a case against us, saying we had given part of the property to someone else without their permission. That case was still going on when, in December 1988, the government changed the rent law. From that point, the law said it would no longer apply to any tenancy where the rent is more than Rs. 3,500 per month. Since our rent is higher than that, the officer who handles rent disputes should no longer have had the power to decide anything about our tenancy.

We told the officer in 1992 that he no longer had authority over our case because of this change in the law, and we asked him to stop the proceedings. But he refused. Then, in 1991, the landlord sent us a notice saying they wanted to end the tenancy. Later, they started another case in a different court to take back the property. We told that court it was not fair to have two cases going on at the same time, especially since the rent law no longer covered us after 1988. The court there did not agree with us and allowed the case to continue.

Now, the landlord is trying to remove us from the property using a process that should no longer apply to us. I feel that once the law changed in 1988, the old case should have ended. The landlord should not be allowed to keep using a system that no longer covers our tenancy.

We have been running our business from this place for a long time. I want to continue doing so without the threat of being thrown out through a process that no longer applies to us. I need your help to stop this and protect our right to stay.

I am one of the guarantors for a loan taken by Ace Concrete Private Limited from Indian Overseas Bank. In 2010, the bank gave the company a loan of Rs. 21.14 crore, and my family and I, along with some other relatives, mortgaged four of our properties to secure it. We also signed personal guarantees for Rs. 22.74 crore. The properties are in and around Chennai — one in Chrompet, another in Kilpauk, and two others nearby. Some are ancestral, some we bought ourselves. We never expected to lose them.

In 2011, the company’s shares and management were supposed to be taken over by a firm called AKR Holdings. They agreed to pay off all the company’s debts and get our properties released. But they didn’t. Instead, they took over, sold off the company’s assets, and walked away. The bank then declared the loan a bad debt and started coming after us, even though the new people were running the company.

On May 23, 2011, the bank sent a notice saying we owed Rs. 20.24 crore. We replied in July 2011, explaining that the new management should be held responsible, not us. But the bank ignored us. By August 2011, they claimed they had taken control of our properties. Then in January 2012, they announced they would sell all four properties, saying the total due was now over Rs. 23 crore.

We objected and asked for time. We managed to sell one of the properties privately and paid Rs. 12.25 crore to the bank by March 2012. We had already paid Rs. 50 lakh earlier. But the bank issued another sale notice in July 2012 for the remaining three properties, now saying the amount was about Rs. 12 crore.

We kept trying to settle, and paid another Rs. 1 crore in July 2012 to show we were serious. But in July 2012, the bank sold two of our properties to a man named N. Subhash Chand Jain for only Rs. 4.86 crore — far less than they were worth. We couldn’t pay the additional amount they later demanded because we were arranging buyers ourselves and had also raised concerns about fraud by some bank officials.

Years passed. In 2018, the officer handling such cases ruled in our favour — he cancelled the sale and told the bank to return the money to the buyer and also refund Rs. 4.48 crore to one of us, Shanthi Sivasamy, with interest. But the bank and the buyer challenged that decision, and in 2019, a higher officer overturned most of it.

Now, the buyer is trying to take possession, and we’re about to lose our homes and lands. We’ve spent years fighting, paid crores, and still face eviction. I want the sale cancelled and our properties returned — or at least get back the excess money we paid. The bank never gave us a fair chance.

I’ve been living in three rooms and a courtyard at Premises Nos. 2216–2222, Gali Inder Chammar Teliwara, Delhi since 1947. Back then, the place was evacuee property, and the government custodian allowed me to stay there as a tenant. I’ve lived there continuously, paid rent regularly, and treated it as my home for over 30 years.

In 1956, the property was bought jointly by Sunder Singh’s father and a woman named Smt. Sham Kaur. I found out later that Smt. Sham Kaur paid half the purchase amount—Rs. 25,700—so they were both owners. I never signed any new agreement with them. No fresh lease was made, and nothing changed in how I occupied the place.

Smt. Sham Kaur passed away in 1975, and her legal heirs became co-owners along with Sunder Singh’s father. But in June 1975, even before she died, Sunder Singh’s father started trying to get me out. He said he needed the house for his family because he didn’t have enough space elsewhere. He claimed he needed it for his wife, three married sons, five daughters, and even for a pooja room and a sitting area. But he didn’t include Smt. Sham Kaur or her heirs in the process.

He served me a notice in 1972 saying he wanted the place back, but I’ve always questioned whether that notice was proper, especially since the property was under government control when I first moved in. Also, rent was paid to him, but that doesn’t mean the other owner gave up their rights. I believe both owners should have to agree if a tenant is to be removed.

One authority looked at my case and said I could stay, agreeing that one owner can’t act alone when there are two. But another body later said I could be evicted based on what the father claimed. I don’t see how one person, without the other owner being involved, can make such a decision about a jointly owned property.

I’ve lived here my whole life. I just want to continue living in my home. I want things to be fair—both owners should have to agree if the tenancy ends. That’s all I’m asking.

I own a piece of land in Village Sayoorpur, about 58 bigha and 14 biswa, which has been with my family for generations. My father, Ishwar Chander Gupta, along with two partners, was one of the owners. The land is part of a larger area around Delhi that the government wanted to develop back in the 1980s.

In 1980, the government put out a public notice saying they intended to take over land in several villages, including ours. Then, years later in 1985, they issued another notice saying the acquisition was moving forward. At that time, we went to court to challenge it, arguing that too much time had passed between the first notice and the second one. Our case was dismissed, but around the same time, many other landowners from nearby villages were fighting similar battles.

By 1988, a decision came out that affected all these cases. It said the government’s action was invalid because landowners weren’t properly heard when they raised objections. After that, in 1989, the authorities admitted they couldn’t take possession of any land unless people who had already taken compensation returned the money with 12% interest. Since we never accepted any money or alternative plots, we believed our land was fully ours again.

In 1990, I sold 28 bigha and 8 biswa of the land through proper sale deeds. The buyer has been in possession since then. But now, the Delhi Development Authority is acting like the acquisition is still active and that they can take the land. I don’t understand how that can happen after everything that was decided. I want to know if my sale is valid and whether I still have the right to my property. I need to protect what my family has held for years.

I’m one of the joint owners of a property in Ashok Vihar, Delhi, numbered 1-87. My brother Rameshwar Dass Gupta and I, along with a few other family members, inherited this property. Over time, we couldn’t agree on how to divide it, so he started a legal process to sort it out. Eventually, it was decided that the property should be sold and the money split among all of us.

After that, the sale was scheduled for January 2010. When I heard about it, I asked the authorities to pause the auction because I wanted to buy the property myself. I live here, and it’s been in our family for years. I told them I was ready to pay my share and even cover the others’ shares so the property wouldn’t go to an outsider. Everyone, including the other owners, agreed in writing, and the sale was put off.

But I couldn’t arrange the full amount right away. Because of that, the sale process started again. It was postponed a couple of times and finally happened on 8 October 2010. A company called J.S. Exim Ltd. says they won it with a bid of Rs. 9.60 crores. They claim they paid Rs. 2.40 crores on the day of the auction through 27 demand drafts, and the rest by 23 October 2010.

I have serious doubts about whether that payment was made properly on the day of the auction. The drafts they used were not issued correctly at the time, and I don’t believe the money was handed over when it should have been. There are rules about this—25% must be paid right after the bidding ends—and I don’t think that happened.

Before the sale was confirmed, I submitted a request on 1 December 2010 asking to be allowed to pay the full amount and keep the property. I’m still ready to do that—even pay more than what was bid, including interest or an extra Rs. 1 crore—because this is my home. But they went ahead and approved the sale without looking at my request.

All I want is a fair chance to pay what’s due and keep the property. I’m not asking for special treatment—just the opportunity to settle everything and stay in the home I’ve lived in for years.

I own a piece of land on Mount Road in Madras. It was originally part of a bigger plot of 41 grounds and 2005 sq. ft., jointly owned by several people, including a man named Ganshyamdas Girdhardas. In 1947, the owners leased two parts of the land to his business, India Automobiles. The first part, Door No. 2, was 4 grounds and 151 sq. ft., rented for Rs. 150 a month. The second, Door No. 3, was 8700 sq. ft., for Rs. 200 a month. At the time, the business was just his, but later, in 1961, it became a partnership with his four sons.

On 30 July 1953, all the co-owners, including Ganshyamdas, sold the entire property — land and buildings — to two insurance companies. I have the sale deed from that date, and it clearly says the buildings were included in the sale. In 1956, I took over those two companies and became the owner of the property.

In July 1965, I applied to the Rent Controller to set a fair rent for both properties because the old rent was far too low. I asked for Rs. 2,399 per month for Door No. 2 and Rs. 3,266 for Door No. 3. The tenants objected, saying they had built the structures themselves on empty land and that only the land was leased, not the buildings. They claimed I had no right to ask for rent on the buildings.

But the Rent Controller looked at the sale deed and said the buildings were part of what was sold to me. Later, when the tenants challenged this, the decision was confirmed — the buildings belonged to me. One of the officers who reviewed the case even noted that earlier rent matters had already treated me as the owner.

After their objections were rejected in 1968, I started a case to recover the unpaid rent based on the fair rent orders. The tenants keep saying they own the buildings, but the documents and past decisions support my claim. I want to recover the rent I’m owed and have my ownership of the buildings recognised. The sale deed and the way things have been treated over the years back me up.

I am the Executive Officer representing the idol of Sri Renganathaswamy at the temple in Srirangam. I’m coming to you because a group calling themselves a trust—Ramanuja Koodam, led by P.K. Thoppulan Chettiar’s descendants—wants to sell a large part of land that rightfully belongs to the temple’s charitable work. This land is in Geethapuram, Melur region, Srirangam, about 25,000 square feet total. On part of it, there’s a black stone hall where the deity was brought during festivals like Chithirai and Gajendra Moksham.

The land was bought in 1887 by Thoppulan Chettiar himself, not for personal use, but specifically to carry out charity connected to our temple. He built the stone hall there and for 14 years, he hosted the idol during festivals, gave water and millet porridge to devotees, and funded it all from his business and the land’s income. Then in 1901, he signed a Deed of Settlement saying this land must never be sold or mortgaged—it was to be used only for continuing those charitable activities. His sons and their descendants were supposed to keep it going, using the land’s income, and if there was extra money, they could save it as a family fund, but only after covering the charity costs.

Now, over a century later, these descendants say they’re struggling—there are encroachments, and they can’t manage the property. So in 2001, they made an agreement to sell 20,865 square feet of this land to a private buyer, keeping only the 4,135 square feet with the stone hall. They claim they want to use the interest from the sale money to fund the charity instead.

But this is wrong. The land was dedicated to the temple’s service. The trust they formed is not a public body—the temple never appointed them, and no one from outside the family runs it. Still, the work they do—feeding devotees, hosting the deity—is part of our temple’s religious festivals. The land isn’t just property; it’s meant for a religious purpose. They don’t have the right to sell it. Only the Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments can allow such a sale, not a civil court. I have the Deed of Settlement, and it clearly shows the land was set aside for the temple’s charity. I want to stop this sale and protect what belongs to the deity and its devotees.

My name is Punithavalli Ammal, and I live in Poongavur village in Tanjavoor District. My father, Somasundara Udayar, passed away long before 1937. After he died, my mother, Sellathachi, took care of his properties — some land and a house. She managed everything on her own. For years, she collected the income, paid the taxes, and made decisions about the property. Everyone in the village knew she was in charge.

In June 1956, something changed. I learned that a new government law had come into effect that gave widows full ownership of their husband’s property. From that point, my mother wasn’t just holding the property — she became its complete owner, with the right to use it, sell it, or give it away as she wished.

A month later, in July 1956, she adopted a boy named Ramalingam. He is the son of my sister Kappaimal. But even after that, my mother remained in full control. Then, in June 1957, she made a formal settlement. She gave me 9 acres and 16 cents of land and half of the house. The deed was properly written and registered. I have a copy of it. The revenue records also show her name as the owner at that time.

But after she did this, Ramalingam’s family started a case. They say that because he was adopted, he automatically gets all rights to my father’s property from the day my father died — even before the adoption happened. They claim that because of this, my mother couldn’t give me any part of the property.

That doesn’t make sense to me. The adoption came after the law changed. My mother was the full owner by then. She had every right to decide who should get what. I want the court to recognize that the settlement she made in my favour is valid. I want to keep the land and half the house that she gave me.
